verse.text: I wrote my first account, Theophilus, about everything that Jesus began both to do and to teach
until the day he was taken up, after giving instructions through the Holy Spirit to the apostles he had chosen.

note.traditional: after he had given commands through the Holy Spirit to the apostles whom he had chosen

verse.note: In the Greek this phrase stands between "giving instructions to the apostles" and "whom he had chosen" and could modify either. Most translations, as here, attach it to the giving of instructions. A minority of interpreters read "the apostles whom he had chosen through the Holy Spirit."

verse.text: To them he also presented himself alive after his suffering by many convincing proofs, appearing to them over forty days and speaking about the kingdom of God.
And while eating with them, he ordered them not to leave Jerusalem but to wait for what the Father had promised, “which you heard about from me;

note.traditional: being assembled together with them / while staying with them

verse.note: The verb is rare and its meaning here is disputed. It may mean "eat together," "gather together," or be a variant spelling of a verb meaning "stay with." The sense "eat with" is how ancient translations such as the Latin took it, and it fits Luke's emphasis on the risen Jesus eating with his disciples (Luke 24:41–43; Acts 10:41). Certainty is not possible.

text.q: for John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now.”

verse.text: So when they had come together, they began asking him, “Lord, is it at this time that you are restoring the kingdom to Israel?”
He said to them, “It is not for you to know times or seasons that the Father has set by his own authority,

text.q: but you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth.”

verse.text: After saying this, he was lifted up while they were watching, and a cloud took him up out of their sight.
And as they were gazing into heaven while he was going, suddenly two men in white clothes were standing beside them,
verse.note: Luke regularly describes angels as men in bright or white clothing. The two "men" at the tomb in Luke 24:4 are called angels in 24:23, and the angel of Acts 10:3 is described as "a man in bright clothing" in 10:30. Readers would have understood these figures as heavenly messengers, though Luke does not use the word here.

verse.text: and they said, “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven.”
Then they returned to Jerusalem from what is called the Mount of Olives, which is near Jerusalem, a sabbath day’s journey away.
verse.note: This is a measure of distance: the farthest one was permitted to walk on the sabbath under Jewish custom. It was about two thousand cubits, roughly a kilometre or a little over half a mile. The phrase does not imply that the events took place on a sabbath.

verse.text: When they had entered the city, they went up to the upstairs room where they were staying: Peter and John and James and Andrew, Philip and Thomas, Bartholomew and Matthew, James son of Alphaeus and Simon the Zealot and Judas son of James.
verse.note: The word means someone zealous or ardently devoted, and Luke uses it elsewhere of zeal for the Law or for God (Acts 21:20; 22:3). Whether it marks Simon as belonging to a revolutionary movement is disputed, since an organised party called the Zealots is clearly attested only from the Jewish war of AD 66–70. The traditional rendering is kept, but it may mean no more than "the zealous one."

verse.text: All these were devoting themselves with one mind to prayer, together with the women and Mary the mother of Jesus, and with his brothers.
In those days Peter stood up among the brothers and sisters (the crowd gathered there numbered about a hundred and twenty people) and said,

note.traditional: the brethren / the brothers (KJV, following a different text: the disciples)

verse.note: The plural of the Greek word for "brother" was the ordinary way to refer to a mixed group of community members, and verse 14 has just said that women were part of this gathering. Many recent translations render it "believers" or "brothers and sisters" for this reason. In verse 16 Peter uses a formal address that is explicitly masculine, and it is translated "Brothers." In verse 14 the same word means Jesus's actual siblings.

text.q: “Brothers, the scripture had to be fulfilled which the Holy Spirit spoke beforehand through the mouth of David about Judas, who became a guide to those who arrested Jesus,
for he was numbered among us and was allotted his share in this service.”

verse.note: The Greek word was an everyday term for service or an assigned task carried out on someone's behalf. "Ministry" is the usual rendering, but it now suggests a clerical profession, which the word did not convey in the first century. The same word recurs in verse 25.

verse.text: Now this man acquired a field with the wages of his wrongdoing, and falling headlong he burst open in the middle, and all his intestines spilled out.

note.term: Now this man acquired a field

verse.note: Verses 18–19 are generally read as an aside by the narrator rather than part of Peter's speech. The phrase "in their own language" and the translation of the Aramaic name are addressed to Luke's readers, not to an audience in Jerusalem. Matthew 27:3–10 gives a different account, in which Judas hangs himself and the chief priests buy the field. How the two accounts relate is debated.

The word normally means "face down" or "headfirst," and that is the rendering of most translations. Some scholars have proposed that it here carries a medical sense, "swollen up," which is how some ancient versions and later traditions about Judas understood the verse. The evidence for that sense is thin, so the usual meaning is kept.

verse.text: This became known to all who live in Jerusalem, so that the field was called in their own language Akeldama, that is, Field of Blood.

text.q: “For it is written in the book of Psalms, ‘Let his homestead become desolate, and let there be no one living in it,’ and, ‘Let another take his position of oversight.’

verse.note: The two quotations are from Psalm 69:25 and Psalm 109:8, in the wording of the Greek version. The first is adapted from the plural ("their homestead") to the singular so that it applies to Judas. "Position of oversight" translates the psalm's word for an assigned charge or office, which older versions rendered "bishoprick" and most modern ones render "office."

text.q: So then, of the men who accompanied us during all the time that the Lord Jesus went in and out among us,
beginning from John’s baptism until the day he was taken up from us, one of these must become a witness with us to his resurrection.”

verse.text: So they put forward two: Joseph called Barsabbas, who was also known as Justus, and Matthias.
And they prayed and said, “You, Lord, who know the hearts of all, show which one of these two you have chosen

text.q: to take the place in this service and apostleship from which Judas turned aside to go to his own place.”

verse.text: And they cast lots for them, and the lot fell on Matthias, and he was counted with the eleven apostles.
verse.note: In Israel's scriptures, casting lots was a recognised way of leaving a decision to God, used for dividing land and assigning priestly duties (compare Proverbs 16:33). The same Greek word lies behind "was allotted his share" in verse 17, so the replacement is chosen by the same means the language of that verse evokes. This is the last time the New Testament reports the practice among Jesus's followers.

verse.text: When the day of Pentecost arrived, they were all together in one place.
verse.note: The word means 'fiftieth' and was the Greek name for the Jewish Feast of Weeks, the harvest festival held on the fiftieth day after Passover. It was one of the three pilgrimage festivals, which helps explain why Jerusalem was so full of Jews from abroad.

verse.text: Suddenly a sound came from heaven like the rush of a violent wind, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting.
And there appeared to them tongues as of fire, divided among them, and one settled on each of them.
They were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other tongues, as the Spirit gave them to speak out.
verse.note: The Greek word means both the tongue as an organ and a language. Verses 6–11 show that real foreign languages, understood by their native speakers, are meant here. 'Tongues' is kept so that the echo of the 'tongues as of fire' in verse 3 is not lost. A minority of scholars think Luke has reshaped an account of ecstatic speech.

verse.text: Now there were Jews living in Jerusalem, devout men from every nation under heaven.
verse.note: The Greek word here is the same one that in the plural is usually translated 'Gentiles', meaning the non-Jewish peoples. Here it plainly means the nations of the world as ethnic and political units, among whom these Jews had been living.

verse.text: At this sound the crowd gathered and was thrown into confusion, because each one heard them speaking in his own language.
They were astounded and amazed, and said, “Look, aren’t all these who are speaking Galileans?

text.q: So how is it that each of us hears them in our own language, the one we were born into?
Parthians and Medes and Elamites, and those who live in Mesopotamia, Judea and Cappadocia, Pontus and Asia,

verse.note: This is the Roman province of Asia, the western part of modern Turkey with Ephesus as its chief city, and not the continent.

text.q: Phrygia and Pamphylia, Egypt and the parts of Libya near Cyrene, and visitors from Rome,
both Jews and converts, Cretans and Arabs—we hear them speaking in our own tongues of the great deeds of God.”

verse.text: They were all astounded and at a loss, saying to one another, “What does this mean?”
But others mocked and said, “They are full of sweet wine.”
But Peter, standing with the eleven, raised his voice and spoke out to them: “Fellow Jews and all you who live in Jerusalem, let this be known to you, and give ear to my words.
verse.note: The Greek is literally 'Men, Jews', a formal style of address also seen in verses 22 and 29. Many translations render it 'Men of Judea', taking the word geographically alongside 'all who live in Jerusalem'. Since verse 5 uses the same word for Jews from every nation now living in the city, the ethnic sense is preferred here, but either is possible.

text.q: These people are not drunk, as you suppose, for it is only the third hour of the day.

note.term: the third hour of the day
note.traditional: the third hour of the day

verse.note: Hours were counted from sunrise, so the third hour is about nine in the morning. Peter's point is that it is far too early in the day for anyone to be drunk.

text.q: No, this is what was spoken through the prophet Joel:

‘And it will be in the last days, God says, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh, and your sons and your daughters will prophesy, and your young men will see visions, and your old men will dream dreams.
Yes, even on my slaves, men and women alike, I will pour out my Spirit in those days, and they will prophesy.

note.term: my slaves, men and women alike
note.traditional: my servants, both men and women (or 'menservants and maidservants')

verse.note: The Greek words are the ordinary masculine and feminine terms for slaves, and a first-century reader would have heard them that way. Most translations soften this to 'servants'. In Joel the line extends the gift of the Spirit down to the lowest social rank; the added 'my' in Acts makes them God's own slaves.

text.q: And I will give wonders in the sky above and signs on the earth below, blood and fire and a cloud of smoke.
The sun will be turned to darkness and the moon to blood before the day of the Lord comes, the great and glorious day.
And it will be that everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.’
Fellow Israelites, hear these words: Jesus of Nazareth, a man attested to you by God with deeds of power and wonders and signs that God did through him among you, as you yourselves know—
this man, handed over by the fixed plan and foreknowledge of God, you nailed up and killed by the hands of lawless men.

verse.note: The word can mean 'wicked' in general or, more specifically, 'those without the Law', that is, Gentiles. Many scholars think the second sense is intended here, pointing to the Romans who carried out the execution. The rendering leaves both possibilities open.

text.q: But God raised him up, bringing the pangs of death to an end, because it was not possible for him to be held by it.

note.traditional: the pains of death / the agony of death

verse.note: The Greek word normally means the pains of childbirth. The phrase comes from the Greek version of the Psalms (for example Psalm 18:4–5), where it translates a Hebrew word that can mean either 'cords' or 'pangs'. Whether Luke intends an image of death in labour, unable to hold back what it must give up, is debated.

text.q: For David says of him: ‘I saw the Lord always before me, for he is at my right hand so that I may not be shaken.
Therefore my heart was glad and my tongue rejoiced, and my flesh too will dwell in hope,
because you will not abandon my soul to Hades, nor will you let your faithful one see decay.

verse.note: This is not the usual Greek word for 'holy' but one meaning devout or loyal to God, used in the Greek Psalms for the Hebrew word for a faithful worshipper. Most translations have 'your Holy One', often capitalised as a title. The rendering here keeps the two Greek words distinct; the quotation is from Psalm 16:8–11.

text.q: You have made known to me the paths of life; you will fill me with gladness in your presence.’
Brothers, I may speak to you plainly about the patriarch David: he both died and was buried, and his tomb is among us to this day.
So, being a prophet, and knowing that God had sworn to him with an oath to seat one from the fruit of his loins on his throne,
he foresaw and spoke about the resurrection of the Messiah, that he was not abandoned to Hades, nor did his flesh see decay.

verse.note: The Greek word means 'anointed one' and here, as in verse 36, it is a title for Israel's expected king, which 'Messiah' conveys more directly than 'Christ'. Where it is attached to Jesus's name, as in verse 38, 'Christ' is kept. Several modern translations make the same distinction.

text.q: This Jesus God raised up, and of that we are all witnesses.
Exalted, then, to the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this that you see and hear.

note.term: to the right hand of God
note.traditional: exalted to (or at) the right hand of God

verse.note: The Greek can equally mean 'exalted by the right hand of God', that is, by God's power. 'To the right hand' is chosen because the psalm quoted in the next verse speaks of sitting at God's right hand, but the other reading has scholarly support.

text.q: For David did not go up into the heavens, but he himself says: ‘The Lord said to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand
until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet.”’
So let the whole house of Israel know for certain that God has made him both Lord and Messiah, this Jesus whom you crucified.”

verse.text: When they heard this they were cut to the heart, and they said to Peter and the rest of the apostles, “Brothers, what should we do?”
Peter said to them, “Turn back, and let each of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.
verse.note: 'Repent' now suggests mainly feeling sorry, whereas the Greek word carries the prophets' call to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct. Most translations keep 'repent' as an established term that readers understand to include a changed life.

text.q: For the promise is for you and for your children and for all who are far away, as many as the Lord our God calls to himself.”

verse.text: With many other words he bore solemn witness and kept urging them, saying, “Be saved from this crooked generation.”
So those who welcomed his word were baptized, and about three thousand people were added that day.
They were devoted to the apostles’ teaching and to the common life, to the breaking of bread and to the prayers.
verse.note: The Greek word means sharing or partnership and is related to the word 'common' in verse 44. 'Fellowship' is the usual rendering, but in modern usage it often suggests little more than social time. Scholars disagree whether the word here refers to the community's bond in general or specifically to the sharing of goods described in the following verses.

verse.text: Awe came over everyone, and many wonders and signs were taking place through the apostles.
All who believed were together and held everything in common,
and they would sell their property and possessions and divide the proceeds among all, as anyone had need.
Day by day they were devoted, with one mind, to being in the temple; and breaking bread in their homes, they shared their food with great joy and simplicity of heart,
praising God and having favor with all the people. And day by day the Lord added to their company those who were being saved.
verse.note: Later manuscripts read 'added to the church', which is the source of the King James wording. The earliest manuscripts lack 'the church' and have only a phrase meaning 'together' or 'to the same group', the same expression used in verses 1 and 44.

verse.text: Now Peter and John were going up to the temple at the hour of prayer, the ninth hour.
verse.note: Hours were counted from sunrise, so the ninth hour is about three in the afternoon. This was the time of the daily afternoon sacrifice in the temple, when people gathered to pray.

verse.text: And a man who had been lame from his mother’s womb was being carried in. Every day they would set him at the gate of the temple called Beautiful, to ask for alms from those going into the temple.

note.term: the gate of the temple called Beautiful
note.traditional: the gate of the temple which is called Beautiful

verse.note: No other ancient source uses this name for a temple gate, and its identification is uncertain. Many scholars connect it with the bronze Nicanor Gate on the east side of the inner courts. Luke uses the word for 'door' here and for 'gate' in verse 10, and both are rendered 'gate'.

verse.text: Seeing Peter and John about to go into the temple, he asked to be given alms.
Peter looked intently at him, as did John, and said, “Look at us.”
He fixed his attention on them, expecting to receive something from them.
But Peter said, “Silver and gold I do not have, but what I do have, this I give you: in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, walk!”
verse.note: Many manuscripts read 'rise up and walk'. The shorter reading translated here is found in some of the earliest witnesses. The longer one may have been influenced by similar commands in the Gospels, though the evidence is divided and some editions print the longer text.

verse.text: And grasping him by the right hand, he raised him up. At once his feet and ankles were made strong,
and leaping up, he stood and began to walk, and he went into the temple with them, walking and leaping and praising God.
And all the people saw him walking and praising God,
and they recognized him as the one who used to sit for alms at the Beautiful Gate of the temple, and they were filled with awe and astonishment at what had happened to him.
While he clung to Peter and John, all the people ran together to them in the colonnade called Solomon’s, awestruck.

note.traditional: the porch that is called Solomon's

verse.note: This was a long roofed walkway lined with columns, running along the eastern side of the temple's outer court. It was a public space where people could gather and teachers could speak.

verse.text: When Peter saw this, he addressed the people: “Israelites, why do you marvel at this, or why do you look so intently at us, as though by our own power or piety we had made him walk?

text.q: The God of Abraham and Isaac and Jacob, the God of our fathers, has glorified his servant Jesus, whom you handed over and disowned in the presence of Pilate, though he had decided to release him.

note.traditional: his Son (KJV); his servant (most modern versions)

verse.note: The Greek word can mean either 'child' or 'servant'. Most scholars take it as 'servant' here, because 'glorified his servant' echoes the Greek version of Isaiah 52:13, the opening of the passage about the suffering servant. Older English versions rendered it 'Son'. The same word recurs in verse 26.

text.q: But you disowned the Holy and Righteous One and asked that a murderer be granted to you,
and you killed the author of life, whom God raised from the dead. Of this we are witnesses.

note.traditional: the Author of life; the Prince of life (KJV)

verse.note: The Greek word covers both a leader who goes first and a founder or originator. It can therefore mean the one who is the source of life or the one who leads the way into life, and translators are divided. 'Author' is used in the sense of originator, not writer. Either way the paradox is deliberate: they killed the one from whom life comes.

text.q: And on the basis of faith in his name, his name has made strong this man whom you see and know; the faith that comes through him has given him this complete health in front of all of you.

note.term: on the basis of faith in his name

verse.note: The Greek sentence is awkward and repetitive, and the translation keeps its structure. It does not say whose faith is meant, the lame man's or the apostles'. 'The faith that comes through him' could also be read as 'the faith that is through it', that is, through the name.

text.q: And now, brothers, I know that you acted in ignorance, as your rulers did too.
But what God announced beforehand through the mouth of all the prophets, that his Messiah would suffer, he has fulfilled in this way.

verse.note: The Greek word is a title meaning the anointed king Israel expected, and here the title itself is the point: that this figure had to suffer. 'Messiah' is used where the word works as a title, and 'Christ' where it is attached to the name Jesus, as in verse 6. Several modern translations make the same distinction.

text.q: Turn back, then, and return, so that your sins may be wiped out,

verse.note: 'Repent' now suggests mainly feeling sorry. The Greek word carries the prophets' call to change direction in mind and conduct and come back to God. Most translations keep 'repent' as an established term. It is paired here with a second verb of turning, rendered 'return', which reinforces the same idea.

text.q: so that seasons of refreshment may come from the presence of the Lord, and that he may send the Messiah appointed for you, Jesus,
whom heaven must receive until the times of the restoration of all that God spoke of through the mouth of his holy prophets from of old.

note.term: the restoration of all that God spoke of
note.traditional: the times of restitution of all things, which God hath spoken

verse.note: The Greek can mean the restoration of all things, a restoration the prophets spoke about. It can also mean the establishment, that is the fulfilment, of everything God spoke through the prophets. The rendering leaves both possibilities open. The noun is related to the verb in the disciples' question about restoring the kingdom to Israel in Acts 1:6.

text.q: Moses said, ‘The Lord God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers. You shall listen to him in everything he says to you.

note.term: The Lord God will raise up for you a prophet like me

verse.note: Peter quotes Deuteronomy 18:15–19, the promise of a prophet like Moses, and joins to it a warning worded like Leviticus 23:29. By the first century many read this promise as pointing to a single coming figure. The verb 'raise up' is the same one used for raising from the dead, and it returns in verse 26.

text.q: And it shall be that every person who does not listen to that prophet will be utterly destroyed from among the people.’
And all the prophets who have spoken, from Samuel and those after him, also announced these days.
You are the sons of the prophets and of the covenant that God made with your fathers, when he said to Abraham, ‘And in your offspring all the families of the earth will be blessed.’
It was to you first that God, having raised up his servant, sent him to bless you by turning each of you away from your wicked deeds.”

note.term: by turning each of you away from your wicked deeds
note.traditional: in turning away every one of you from his iniquities

verse.note: The Greek verb can be taken as transitive, with God's servant turning each person away from wickedness, as translated here. It can also be intransitive: 'as each of you turns away from your wicked deeds'. Most translations take it as transitive.

verse.text: While they were speaking to the people, the priests and the captain of the temple and the Sadducees came upon them,
verse.note: This was a senior priestly official responsible for order in the temple precincts and for its Levite police. He was a Jewish officer, not a Roman one, and is commonly identified with the official whom later Jewish sources rank next to the high priest.

verse.text: greatly annoyed that they were teaching the people and proclaiming in Jesus the resurrection from the dead,
and they seized them and put them in custody until the next day, for it was already evening.
But many of those who heard the word believed, and the number of the men came to about five thousand.
On the next day their rulers and elders and scribes assembled in Jerusalem,
together with Annas the high priest, and Caiaphas, John, Alexander, and all who belonged to the high-priestly family.
verse.note: Annas had held the office years earlier (about AD 6–15) before being removed by the Roman governor. The serving high priest at this time was his son-in-law Caiaphas. Luke gives Annas the title anyway, as in Luke 3:2, probably reflecting his continuing authority as head of the dominant high-priestly family. The John and Alexander named here are otherwise unknown.

verse.text: They had them stand in the middle and began to question them: “By what power or in what name did you do this?”
Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, said to them, “Rulers of the people and elders,

text.q: if we are being examined today about a good deed done to a disabled man, and by what means this man has been made well,

note.traditional: is made whole / has been healed

verse.note: The Greek verb covers both healing and rescue. It is the same verb translated “saved” in verse 12, where the related noun is “salvation.” Peter's speech moves deliberately from the man's cure to salvation in the widest sense, and English needs two words where Greek has one.

text.q: let it be known to all of you and to all the people of Israel that in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead—by him this man stands before you healthy.
He is the stone that was scorned by you, the builders, which has become the cornerstone.

verse.note: Peter adapts Psalm 118:22, sharpening “rejected” to “scorned” and adding “by you.” The Greek is literally “head of the corner,” which may be a foundation stone at the corner of a building or the final stone that crowns a wall or arch. Scholars are divided; either way it is the stone on which the structure depends.

text.q: And salvation is in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among people by which we must be saved.”

verse.text: Seeing the boldness of Peter and John, and realizing that they were unschooled, ordinary men, they were amazed, and they recognized that they had been with Jesus.
verse.note: The first word often means “illiterate” in documents of the period, but here it most likely means that they lacked formal training in the Law such as scribes had. The second word (idiōtēs) means a layperson, someone without professional or official standing, and does not imply stupidity. The council's surprise is that men without credentials speak so confidently.

verse.text: And seeing the man who had been healed standing with them, they had nothing to say in reply.
So they ordered them to go outside the council and conferred with one another,
saying, “What are we to do with these men? For that a notable sign has taken place through them is plain to everyone living in Jerusalem, and we cannot deny it.

text.q: But so that it spreads no further among the people, let us threaten them not to speak any longer in this name to anyone at all.”

verse.text: So they called them in and ordered them not to utter a word or teach at all in the name of Jesus.
But Peter and John answered them, “Whether it is right in God’s sight to listen to you rather than to God, judge for yourselves;
verse.note: This word is elsewhere rendered “righteous” or “just.” Here it stands in the ordinary Greek idiom “it is right to do something,” where neither of those is natural English. Nearly all translations have “right.”

text.q: for we cannot keep from speaking about what we have seen and heard.”

verse.text: After threatening them further, they released them, finding no way to punish them because of the people, since everyone was glorifying God for what had happened;
for the man on whom this sign of healing had been done was more than forty years old.
After they were released, they went to their own people and reported everything the chief priests and the elders had said to them.
When they heard it, they raised their voice to God with one accord and said, “Master, you who made heaven and earth and the sea and everything in them,
verse.note: This is not the usual word for “Lord,” which appears in verse 29. It is the term for the master of a household or the owner of slaves, and it was used in prayer, including in the Septuagint, for God as absolute ruler. It matches the believers' description of themselves as “slaves” in verse 29.

text.q: who said by the Holy Spirit through the mouth of our father David, your servant: ‘Why did the Gentiles rage, and the peoples plot empty things?

note.term: who said by the Holy Spirit through the mouth of our father David, your servant
note.traditional: who by the mouth of thy servant David hast said

verse.note: The Greek of the earliest manuscripts is grammatically tangled here, with “of our father,” “through the Holy Spirit” and “by the mouth of David” piled together. Many scholars suspect a very early copying error. Later manuscripts have a shorter, smoother form without “our father” and “the Holy Spirit,” which older English versions follow. The translation gives the probable sense of the earlier text.

The quotation is Psalm 2:1–2. One Greek word means both “nations” and, in the plural, the non-Jewish peoples, so “the nations” is equally possible in the psalm itself. “Gentiles” is used because verse 27 applies the psalm term by term, with the same word for the Romans alongside “the peoples of Israel,” and Herod and Pilate as the kings and rulers.

text.q: The kings of the earth took their stand, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Messiah.’

verse.note: The Greek christos means “anointed one” and is the word English borrows as “Christ.” In the psalm it is a title for God's anointed king, so “Messiah” is used here, as in several modern translations; others have “his Anointed.” The prayer picks the word up at once: “whom you anointed” in verse 27 is the related verb.

text.q: For truly in this city there gathered against your holy servant Jesus, whom you anointed, both Herod and Pontius Pilate, with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel,

verse.note: The Greek word can mean either “child” or “servant.” It is the same word used of David in verse 25, and the Septuagint uses it for the servant of the Lord in Isaiah. Most modern translations and scholars read “servant” here; “child” is the older English rendering.

text.q: to do everything that your hand and your plan had determined beforehand should happen.
And now, Lord, look upon their threats, and grant to your slaves to speak your word with all boldness,

verse.note: This is the ordinary word for a slave, a person who belongs to a master. It is a different word from the one translated “servant” in verses 25, 27 and 30. In the Septuagint it is also an honourable way of describing those who belong wholly to God. Most English translations soften it to “servants.”

text.q: while you stretch out your hand to heal, and signs and wonders take place through the name of your holy servant Jesus.”

verse.text: When they had prayed, the place where they were gathered was shaken, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began speaking the word of God with boldness.
Now the whole body of those who believed was one in heart and soul, and not one of them said that anything he owned was his own, but they held everything in common.
With great power the apostles kept giving their testimony to the resurrection of the Lord Jesus, and great grace was upon them all.
For there was no one in need among them, because all who were owners of lands or houses would sell them and bring the proceeds of what was sold
and lay them at the apostles’ feet, and it was distributed to each according to what anyone needed.
Joseph, whom the apostles called Barnabas, which translated means Son of Encouragement, a Levite, a Cypriot by birth,
verse.note: The Greek noun covers encouragement, exhortation and comfort, so “son of consolation” or “son of exhortation” is also possible. “Son of” is a Semitic idiom for someone marked by a quality. How the name Barnabas yields this meaning in Aramaic is uncertain and debated.

verse.text: sold a field that belonged to him, brought the money, and laid it at the apostles’ feet.
But a man named Ananias, together with his wife Sapphira, sold a piece of property,
and he kept back some of the price for himself, with his wife fully aware of it, and he brought just a part and laid it at the apostles’ feet.

note.term: kept back some of the price for himself
note.traditional: kept back part of the price

verse.note: The verb means quietly setting aside for oneself what belongs to a common fund; in Titus 2:10 it describes pilfering. The Greek version of Joshua uses it for Achan's theft of goods devoted to God (Joshua 7:1), and many scholars think Luke intends the echo. As Peter says in verse 4, the offence is the deception, not the failure to give everything.

verse.text: But Peter said, “Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart, so that you lied to the Holy Spirit and kept back for yourself some of the price of the land?

text.q: While it remained unsold, did it not remain yours? And once it was sold, was it not at your disposal? Why is it that you set this deed in your heart? You have not lied to people but to God.”

verse.text: As Ananias heard these words, he fell down and breathed his last. And great fear came on all who heard of it.
The younger men got up, wrapped him up, carried him out, and buried him.
After an interval of about three hours his wife came in, not knowing what had happened.
Peter addressed her: “Tell me, did you two sell the land for this much?” She said, “Yes, for that much.”
Then Peter said to her, “Why is it that you agreed together to test the Spirit of the Lord? Look, the feet of those who buried your husband are at the door, and they will carry you out.”
At once she fell down at his feet and breathed her last. When the young men came in they found her dead, and they carried her out and buried her beside her husband.
And great fear came on the whole assembly and on all who heard of these things.
verse.note: A first-century hearer knew this word as a civic gathering and as the Septuagint's term for Israel assembled before God. 'Church' is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. This translation uses 'assembly' throughout so that the reader can see it is one Greek word.

verse.text: Through the hands of the apostles many signs and wonders were taking place among the people. And they were all together, with one mind, in Solomon’s Colonnade.
None of the rest dared to join them, but the people held them in high honor,
verse.note: It is disputed who 'the rest' are and what they did not dare to do. Most take them as outsiders who kept a respectful distance from the group in the colonnade, in contrast with those who came to believe (verse 14). Others take them as the other believers, who did not presume to stand alongside the apostles. The Greek does not settle it.

verse.text: and all the more, believers in the Lord were being added, multitudes of both men and women,

note.term: believers in the Lord were being added
note.traditional: believers were the more added to the Lord

verse.note: 'The Lord' can go with either word: 'those believing in the Lord were added' or 'believers were added to the Lord'. Both readings are grammatical and both are found in the major translations.

verse.text: so that people even carried the sick out into the streets and laid them on cots and mats, so that as Peter came by at least his shadow might fall on some of them.
The multitude from the towns around Jerusalem also kept gathering, bringing the sick and those tormented by unclean spirits, and they were all healed.
Then the high priest rose up, and all who were with him, that is, the party of the Sadducees, and they were filled with jealousy,
and they laid hands on the apostles and put them in public custody.
But during the night an angel of the Lord opened the doors of the prison, led them out, and said,

text.q: “Go, take your stand in the temple and speak to the people all the words of this life.”

verse.text: When they heard this, they entered the temple at daybreak and began teaching. When the high priest and those with him arrived, they called together the council, that is, the whole body of elders of the sons of Israel, and sent to the jail to have them brought.

note.term: that is, the whole body of elders

verse.note: The Greek has 'the council and the whole body of elders'. Most scholars take 'and' as explanatory, with the second phrase describing the council in the language the Septuagint uses for Israel's elders. The alternative reads two bodies, the council plus a wider gathering of elders.

verse.text: But when the officers arrived, they did not find them in the prison. They went back and reported,

text.q: “We found the jail locked with all security and the guards standing at the doors, but when we opened them we found no one inside.”

verse.text: When the captain of the temple and the chief priests heard these words, they were completely at a loss about them, wondering what this might lead to.
Then someone arrived and reported to them, “Look, the men you put in the prison are standing in the temple and teaching the people.”
Then the captain went off with the officers and brought them, but not by force, for they were afraid of being stoned by the people.
They brought them and stood them before the council. And the high priest questioned them,
saying, “We gave you strict orders not to teach in this name, and look, you have filled Jerusalem with your teaching, and you intend to bring this man’s blood on us.”
Peter and the apostles answered, “We must obey God rather than people.
verse.note: The Greek word means human beings in general, not males. The contrast is between divine and human authority, and the same word is rendered 'people' in verses 4 and 38.

text.q: The God of our fathers raised Jesus, whom you killed by hanging him on a tree.

verse.note: The word means wood or anything made of it: a tree, a pole, a beam. Here it refers to the cross. The phrasing echoes Deuteronomy 21:22–23, where a body hung on a tree is under God's curse, and 'tree' is kept so the echo can be heard.

text.q: God exalted this man to his right hand as Leader and Savior, to give Israel turning back and forgiveness of sins.

verse.note: 'Repentance' now centres on feeling sorry. The Greek word carries the prophets' call to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct. Most translations keep 'repentance' as an established term that readers understand to include a change of life.

note.traditional: with his right hand / to his right hand

verse.note: The Greek can mean 'to his right hand', the place of honor, or 'by his right hand', the instrument of God's power. Translations are divided. The same phrase and the same ambiguity occur at Acts 2:33.

text.q: And we are witnesses of these things, and so is the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey him.”

verse.text: When they heard this they were infuriated and wanted to kill them.
But a Pharisee in the council named Gamaliel, a teacher of the law honored by all the people, stood up and ordered the men to be put outside for a little while.
And he said to them, “Men of Israel, take care what you are about to do with these men.

text.q: For some time ago Theudas rose up, claiming to be somebody, and a number of men, about four hundred, attached themselves to him. He was killed, and all who were persuaded by him were dispersed and came to nothing.

verse.note: Josephus describes a Theudas who led a popular movement and was killed under the governor Fadus, around AD 44–46. That is later than the setting of this speech and later than Judas the Galilean (AD 6), whom Gamaliel places after him. Some conclude that Luke's chronology is mistaken here; others suppose an earlier, otherwise unknown Theudas. The question is unresolved.

text.q: After him Judas the Galilean rose up in the days of the census and drew people away after him. He too perished, and all who were persuaded by him were scattered.

verse.note: This is the registration for taxation carried out in AD 6 under Quirinius, when Judea came under direct Roman rule. Josephus reports that Judas led resistance to it on the ground that submitting to Roman taxation was disloyalty to God.

text.q: So now I tell you, keep away from these men and leave them alone—because if this plan or this work is from people, it will be overthrown,

verse.text: but if it is from God, you will not be able to overthrow them—or you may even be found fighting against God.” They were persuaded by him,
and after calling in the apostles they had them flogged, ordered them not to speak in the name of Jesus, and released them.
So they went out from the presence of the council rejoicing that they had been counted worthy to be dishonored for the sake of the Name.
And every day, in the temple and from house to house, they did not stop teaching and proclaiming the good news that the Messiah is Jesus.
verse.note: The Greek has 'the Christ' with the article followed by 'Jesus'. In Acts this marks a title, and the claim being announced is that the expected Messiah is Jesus. Older versions render it as the name 'Jesus Christ'; several modern translations have 'Jesus is the Messiah' or 'Jesus as the Christ'.

verse.text: Now in those days, as the disciples were multiplying, there was grumbling from the Hellenists against the Hebrews, because their widows were being overlooked in the daily serving.
verse.note: Both groups are Jewish followers of Jesus in Jerusalem. On the usual view the Hellenists were Jews whose first language was Greek, many of them from the diaspora, while the Hebrews spoke Aramaic or Hebrew. The word is rare and its exact scope is debated, but a difference of language and culture within the community is the standard explanation.

Most translations have 'distribution', which fits the situation (regular support for widows, in food or money). The Greek noun is the ordinary word for service, and Luke repeats it deliberately: the widows are missed in the daily 'serving', the Twelve will not 'serve' at tables, and they devote themselves to the 'service' of the word. The rendering keeps that thread visible.

verse.text: So the Twelve summoned the whole body of the disciples and said, “It is not acceptable for us to abandon the word of God to serve at tables.
verse.note: The word for table was used both of a dining table and of a money-changer's or banker's counter. The phrase may therefore mean serving food at meals or administering the funds from which the widows were supported. Most interpreters think of meals, but the financial sense is possible.

text.q: So, brothers and sisters, look for seven men from among you who are well spoken of, full of the Spirit and of wisdom, whom we will appoint over this duty.

verse.note: The Greek plural was the normal way to address a mixed group and did not exclude women; here the whole body of disciples is being addressed. Many translations keep 'brothers'. The seven to be chosen, by contrast, are specified as men with a word that means adult males.

text.q: But we will devote ourselves to prayer and to the service of the word.”

verse.text: The proposal pleased the whole body, and they chose Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit, and Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas, and Nicolaus, a proselyte from Antioch.
verse.note: A proselyte was a Gentile who had fully converted to Judaism. Nicolaus is the only one of the seven so described, which implies the others were Jews by birth. All seven names are Greek, which is often taken as a sign that they came from the Hellenist group, though Greek names were common among Jews generally.

verse.text: These they stood before the apostles, and after praying they laid their hands on them.

note.term: after praying they laid their hands on them
note.traditional: and when they had prayed, they laid their hands on them

verse.note: The Greek does not change subject, so grammatically the ones who pray and lay on hands could be the whole community that chose the seven. Most interpreters take the apostles to be the subject, as the nearest noun and in line with verse 3. The translation leaves the wording as open as the Greek.

verse.text: And the word of God kept growing, and the number of the disciples in Jerusalem multiplied greatly, and a large crowd of the priests were becoming obedient to the faith.
Now Stephen, full of grace and power, was doing great wonders and signs among the people.
Then some of those from what was called the Synagogue of the Freedmen, Cyrenians and Alexandrians, and of those from Cilicia and Asia, rose up and began arguing with Stephen,

note.term: the Synagogue of the Freedmen, Cyrenians and Alexandrians, and of those from Cilicia and Asia
note.traditional: the synagogue of the Libertines (Freedmen), and Cyrenians, and Alexandrians, and of them of Cilicia and of Asia

verse.note: The grammar leaves it unclear how many synagogues are meant: one with members from all these places, two (as rendered here, following the two groupings in the Greek), or as many as five. 'Freedmen' is a Latin loanword for former slaves or their descendants, probably Jews whose families had been taken to Rome as captives and later released. Asia here is the Roman province in what is now western Turkey.

verse.text: but they were not able to stand against the wisdom and the Spirit with which he was speaking.
verse.note: The Greek could mean the Holy Spirit or Stephen's own spirit, that is, the force with which he spoke. Since Stephen has just been described as full of the Holy Spirit, the translation takes it as the Spirit; translations are divided.

verse.text: Then they secretly put men up to saying, “We have heard him speaking blasphemous words against Moses and God.”
They stirred up the people, the elders and the scribes, and coming upon him they seized him and brought him to the council.
verse.note: This is the Sanhedrin, the supreme Jewish council in Jerusalem, presided over by the high priest. It is the same body that had tried Jesus and had recently flogged the apostles.

verse.text: They put forward false witnesses who said, “This man never stops speaking words against the holy place and the law,
verse.note: The holy place is the Jerusalem temple. The charge that Jesus would destroy it resembles the accusation Mark and Matthew report at Jesus's own trial, which they too attribute to false witnesses. Some manuscripts read 'this holy place'; the text translated here lacks 'this'.

text.q: for we have heard him say that this Jesus the Nazarene will destroy this place and change the customs that Moses handed down to us.”

verse.text: And all who were sitting in the council, gazing intently at him, saw that his face was like the face of an angel.
Then the high priest said, “Are these things so?”
And he said, “Brothers and fathers, listen. The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham when he was in Mesopotamia, before he settled in Haran,

text.q: and said to him, ‘Leave your land and your relatives, and come to the land that I will show you.’
Then he left the land of the Chaldeans and settled in Haran. And from there, after his father died, God resettled him in this land in which you now live.
He gave him no inheritance in it, not even a foot’s length, yet he promised to give it to him as a possession, and to his descendants after him, though he had no child.
And God spoke in this way: his descendants would be foreigners in a land belonging to others, who would enslave them and mistreat them for four hundred years.
‘But the nation they serve as slaves I myself will judge,’ God said, ‘and after that they will come out and worship me in this place.’

verse.note: The Greek word here is the same one that in the plural is often translated 'Gentiles', meaning the non-Jewish peoples. In this chapter it refers to peoples as ethnic or political units (Egypt here, the Canaanite peoples in verse 45), so 'nation' and 'nations' are used.

text.q: And he gave him a covenant of circumcision. And so Abraham fathered Isaac and circumcised him on the eighth day, and Isaac fathered Jacob, and Jacob the twelve patriarchs.
The patriarchs, jealous of Joseph, sold him into Egypt. But God was with him,
and rescued him from all his afflictions, and gave him favor and wisdom before Pharaoh king of Egypt, who appointed him governor over Egypt and over his whole household.

verse.note: The Greek says only 'and he appointed him', and the subject could be either God or Pharaoh. The translation follows the Genesis story, in which Pharaoh sets Joseph over Egypt and over his own household. If God is the subject, the sense is that God brought the appointment about.

text.q: Then a famine came over all Egypt and Canaan, and great affliction, and our fathers could find no food.
But when Jacob heard that there was grain in Egypt, he sent our fathers there a first time.
On the second visit Joseph made himself known to his brothers, and Joseph’s family became known to Pharaoh.
Then Joseph sent and summoned his father Jacob and all his relatives, seventy-five persons in all,

verse.note: The Hebrew text of Genesis 46:27 and Exodus 1:5 counts seventy. The ancient Greek translation of those passages, the Septuagint, counts seventy-five, and Stephen's figure follows it.

text.q: and Jacob went down to Egypt. And he died, he and our fathers,
and they were carried over to Shechem and laid in the tomb that Abraham had bought for a sum of silver from the sons of Hamor in Shechem.

note.term: the tomb that Abraham had bought

verse.note: In Genesis, Abraham buys a burial cave near Hebron from Ephron the Hittite (Genesis 23), while it is Jacob who buys land at Shechem from the sons of Hamor (Genesis 33:19), where Joseph is later buried (Joshua 24:32). Stephen's compressed summary runs the two purchases together. Interpreters differ on whether this is deliberate telescoping or a slip, and the translation leaves the wording as it stands.

text.q: But as the time of the promise that God had made to Abraham drew near, the people grew and multiplied in Egypt,
until another king arose over Egypt, who did not know Joseph.
He dealt craftily with our people and mistreated our fathers, making them abandon their infants so that they would not survive.
At that time Moses was born, and he was beautiful in God’s sight. He was raised for three months in his father’s house,

verse.note: The Greek is literally 'beautiful to God'. It may mean that God regarded the child as beautiful, or it may be a Semitic way of expressing a superlative, 'extraordinarily beautiful', as when the Greek of Jonah 3:3 calls Nineveh 'a city great to God'. Scholars are divided, and the translation keeps the reference to God.

text.q: and when he was abandoned, Pharaoh’s daughter took him up and raised him as her own son.
So Moses was educated in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, and he was powerful in his words and deeds.
When he was reaching the age of forty, it came into his heart to visit his brothers, the sons of Israel.
Seeing one of them being wronged, he came to his defense and avenged the oppressed man by striking down the Egyptian.
He supposed that his brothers would understand that God was giving them deliverance by his hand, but they did not understand.
The next day he appeared to them as they were fighting and tried to reconcile them, saying, ‘Men, you are brothers. Why are you wronging one another?’
But the one who was wronging his neighbor pushed him away, saying, ‘Who appointed you ruler and judge over us?
Do you want to kill me the way you killed the Egyptian yesterday?’
At this word Moses fled and became a foreigner in the land of Midian, where he fathered two sons.
When forty years had passed, an angel appeared to him in the wilderness of Mount Sinai, in the flame of a burning bush.
When Moses saw it, he was amazed at the sight, and as he came near to look, the voice of the Lord came:
‘I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham and Isaac and Jacob.’ Moses began to tremble and did not dare to look.
Then the Lord said to him, ‘Take the sandals off your feet, for the place where you are standing is holy ground.
I have surely seen the mistreatment of my people in Egypt, and I have heard their groaning, and I have come down to rescue them. And now come, I will send you to Egypt.’
This Moses, whom they disowned, saying, ‘Who appointed you ruler and judge?’—this man God sent as both ruler and redeemer, by the hand of the angel who appeared to him in the bush.
This man led them out, performing wonders and signs in the land of Egypt and at the Red Sea and in the wilderness for forty years.
This is the Moses who said to the sons of Israel, ‘God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers.’
This is the one who was in the assembly in the wilderness with the angel who spoke to him on Mount Sinai and with our fathers, and who received living oracles to give to us.

verse.note: This is the word that English Bibles usually translate 'church'. To a first-century reader it meant a gathering of citizens, and in the Septuagint it is the term for Israel assembled before God, as at Sinai. This translation renders it 'assembly' everywhere so that the reader can see it is one Greek word; many modern versions also use 'assembly' or 'congregation' in this verse.

text.q: Our fathers were unwilling to obey him. Instead they pushed him away and in their hearts turned back to Egypt,
saying to Aaron, ‘Make us gods who will go before us; for this Moses, who led us out of the land of Egypt—we do not know what has happened to him.’
And in those days they made a calf and offered a sacrifice to the idol, and they rejoiced in the works of their hands.

But God turned away and handed them over to worship the host of heaven, as it is written in the book of the prophets: ‘Did you bring me slaughtered animals and sacrifices for forty years in the wilderness, house of Israel?
You took up the tent of Moloch and the star of the god Rephan, the images you made to bow down to them. And I will resettle you beyond Babylon.’

verse.note: Verses 42–43 quote Amos 5:25–27 in its ancient Greek form, which differs from the Hebrew in the names of the gods. Amos says 'beyond Damascus', threatening the northern kingdom with Assyrian exile. Stephen's 'Babylon' reflects the later exile of Judah, which his hearers looked back on as the defining judgment.

text.q: Our fathers had the tent of testimony in the wilderness, just as the one who spoke to Moses directed him to make it, according to the pattern he had seen.

Our fathers in their turn received it and brought it in with Joshua when they took possession of the land of the nations that God drove out before our fathers, and so it remained until the days of David,

verse.note: In Greek the names Joshua and Jesus are identical. The context shows that Moses' successor is meant, but a Greek reader would have seen the same name that Stephen's Lord bears.

text.q: who found favor before God and asked to find a dwelling place for the God of Jacob.

verse.note: Several of the earliest manuscripts read 'for the house of Jacob' instead of 'for the God of Jacob', and some critical editions print that reading as the harder one. The SBLGNT, followed here, reads 'God', which fits the echo of Psalm 132:5. The difference affects whether David sought a dwelling for God or a place of worship for the people.

text.q: But it was Solomon who built him a house.
Yet the Most High does not live in what is made by hands, as the prophet says:

verse.note: In the Septuagint this adjective is the regular term for idols, things made by human hands. Applying it to the Jerusalem temple, just after the golden calf has been called 'the works of their hands', would have struck Stephen's hearers as highly provocative. The quotation that follows is Isaiah 66:1–2.

text.q: ‘Heaven is my throne, and the earth is the footstool of my feet. What kind of house will you build for me, says the Lord, or what is the place of my rest?
Did not my hand make all these things?’
You stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit. As your fathers did, so do you.
Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? They killed those who announced beforehand the coming of the Righteous One, whose betrayers and murderers you have now become,
you who received the law by the direction of angels, and did not keep it.”

verse.note: The Greek phrase is compressed, literally 'as ordinances of angels', and its exact force is debated. It reflects a Jewish tradition that angels were God's agents in giving the law at Sinai, also found in Galatians 3:19 and Hebrews 2:2. Some translate 'as delivered by angels' or 'as ordained by angels'; the point in each case is the law's exalted origin, which makes the failure to keep it worse.

verse.text: When they heard these things, they were torn with rage in their hearts and ground their teeth at him.
But he, full of the Holy Spirit, gazed into heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God,
and he said, “Look, I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God.”
But they cried out with a loud voice, covered their ears, and rushed at him as one,
and they threw him out of the city and began to stone him. And the witnesses laid their cloaks at the feet of a young man called Saul.
verse.note: Under the law, the witnesses whose testimony condemned a person were to throw the first stones (Deuteronomy 17:7). They removed their outer garments to free their arms. These are the witnesses of 6:13, whom the narrator has called false.

verse.text: And they kept stoning Stephen as he called out and said, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.”
Then he knelt down and cried out with a loud voice, “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” And having said this, he fell asleep.
And Saul approved of his killing. On that day a great persecution broke out against the assembly in Jerusalem, and all were scattered throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria, except the apostles.
verse.note: The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering and, in the Greek Old Testament, for Israel assembled before God. 'Church' is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. This translation uses 'assembly' everywhere so that the reader can see it is one Greek word.

verse.text: Devout men buried Stephen and made a great lamentation over him.
But Saul was ravaging the assembly: entering house after house, he dragged off both men and women and handed them over to prison.
Now those who had been scattered went from place to place announcing the good news of the word.
Philip went down to the city of Samaria and proclaimed the Messiah to them.
verse.note: Here the word has the article and is a title, the anointed king Israel expected, not a name for Jesus. This translation uses 'Messiah' where the title is the point and 'Christ' where it works as a name, as in 'Jesus Christ' in verse 12. Several modern translations make the same distinction.

verse.text: The crowds with one accord paid attention to what Philip was saying, as they heard him and saw the signs he was doing.
For unclean spirits, crying out with a loud voice, came out of many who had them, and many who were paralyzed or lame were healed.
So there was great joy in that city.
Now a man named Simon had already been in the city for some time, practicing magic and astonishing the nation of Samaria, claiming to be someone great.
verse.note: The Greek word is the same one that in the plural is usually rendered 'Gentiles'. In the singular it means a people as an ethnic or political unit, and this translation uses 'nation' for that sense. Luke is presenting the Samaritans as a distinct people.

verse.text: They all paid attention to him, from the least to the greatest, saying, “This man is the Power of God that is called Great.”

note.term: the Power of God that is called Great

verse.note: 'Power' could be used as a title for God or for a divine being, so the crowds are claiming that the supreme divine power is present in Simon, not merely that he is impressive. Exactly what Samaritans meant by the title is uncertain. Christian writers from the second century onward remembered Simon as someone his followers revered as divine.

verse.text: They paid attention to him because for a long time he had astonished them with his magic arts.
But when they believed Philip as he announced the good news about the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ, they were baptized, both men and women.
Even Simon himself believed, and after being baptized he stayed close to Philip; and seeing signs and great works of power taking place, he was astonished.
verse.note: Most translations have 'miracles' or 'mighty works'. The Greek is the plural of the word used for Simon in verse 10, and 'astonished' is the word used there for his effect on the crowds. The rendering keeps that echo: the man hailed as the great Power is himself astonished by great works of power.

verse.text: When the apostles in Jerusalem heard that Samaria had accepted the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them,
who went down and prayed for them, that they might receive the Holy Spirit;
for the Spirit had not yet fallen on any of them; they had only been baptized into the name of the Lord Jesus.
Then they laid their hands on them, and they received the Holy Spirit.
When Simon saw that the Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles’ hands, he offered them money,
saying, “Give me this authority too, so that anyone I lay my hands on may receive the Holy Spirit.”
But Peter said to him, “May your silver go with you to destruction, because you thought you could acquire the gift of God with money!

text.q: You have no part or share in this matter, for your heart is not straight before God.

verse.note: The Greek noun can mean 'matter, affair' or 'word, message'. Most translations take it as the matter in hand, the giving of the Spirit. Since the same noun is used in this chapter for the gospel message (verses 4, 14, 25), Peter may instead be saying that Simon has no share 'in this message'. 'No part or share' echoes Old Testament language about having no allotted inheritance.

text.q: So turn back from this wickedness of yours, and beg the Lord that the intent of your heart might perhaps be forgiven you.

verse.note: 'Repent' is the established rendering, and most translations keep it as including a change of life. In current English it centres on feeling sorry, whereas the Greek word carries the prophets' call to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct. 'Turn back' is used to convey that.

text.q: For I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and the bond of wrongdoing.”

note.term: the gall of bitterness and the bond of wrongdoing
note.traditional: the gall of bitterness and the bond of iniquity

verse.note: Both phrases echo the Greek Old Testament. The first recalls the warning in Deuteronomy 29:18 about a root that grows up into gall and bitterness, an image for someone who turns away from God and poisons the community. The second recalls the 'bonds of injustice' in Isaiah 58:6. The Greek preposition could also mean that Simon is headed for this condition rather than already in it.

verse.text: Simon answered, “You yourselves beg the Lord for me, so that nothing of what you have said may come upon me.”
So then, when they had solemnly testified and spoken the word of the Lord, they made their way back to Jerusalem, announcing the good news to many villages of the Samaritans.
Now an angel of the Lord spoke to Philip, saying, “Get up and go toward the south, to the road that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza.” This is a wilderness road.
verse.note: The Greek phrase literally refers to midday and can mean either 'toward the south' or 'at about noon'. Most translations take it as the direction, which suits the route from Jerusalem to Gaza. Some interpreters prefer 'at noon', which would make the command more striking, since travellers avoided the midday heat.

The Greek does not mark whether this sentence is the end of the angel's words or an aside by the narrator; it is taken here as the narrator's. The word means 'deserted, uninhabited' and grammatically could describe either the road or Gaza itself, since the old city had been destroyed, but most interpreters take it of the road.

verse.text: So he got up and went. And there was an Ethiopian man, a eunuch, a high official of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, who was in charge of all her treasure. He had come to Jerusalem to worship,
verse.note: 'Ethiopia' in Greek usage was the kingdom on the Nile south of Egypt with its capital at Meroe, in what is now Sudan, not the modern country of Ethiopia. 'Candace' was understood by Greek and Roman writers as a dynastic title borne by the queens of that kingdom and not as a personal name. To Mediterranean readers this was the far southern edge of the known world.

Royal courts often employed castrated men in positions of trust. The word could occasionally be used loosely for a court official, but as 'high official' follows separately it is probably literal here. Deuteronomy 23:1 barred such men from the assembly of Israel, while Isaiah 56:3–5 promises eunuchs who hold to God's covenant a place in his house. Luke does not say whether this man was a convert to Judaism or a Gentile worshipper of Israel's God.

verse.text: and he was returning, sitting in his chariot and reading the prophet Isaiah.
The Spirit said to Philip, “Go over and stay close to this chariot.”
Philip ran up and heard him reading Isaiah the prophet, and he said, “Do you really understand what you are reading?”
He said, “How could I, unless someone guides me?” And he invited Philip to come up and sit with him.
Now the passage of scripture he was reading was this: “Like a sheep he was led to slaughter, and like a lamb silent before its shearer, so he does not open his mouth.

text.q: In his humiliation justice was taken away from him. Who will describe his generation? For his life is taken away from the earth.”

note.term: justice was taken away from him

verse.note: The quotation is Isaiah 53:7–8 in the ancient Greek version, which differs from the Hebrew. The Greek says literally 'his judgment was taken away', which may mean he was denied a fair trial, as rendered here, or that the sentence against him was lifted. 'His generation' is likewise open: it may refer to his contemporaries, his descendants, or his origin.

verse.text: The eunuch spoke up and said to Philip, “I beg you, about whom does the prophet say this? About himself, or about someone else?”
Then Philip opened his mouth and, beginning from this scripture, announced to him the good news of Jesus.
As they were going along the road, they came to some water, and the eunuch said, “Look, water! What prevents me from being baptized?”

note.term: What prevents me from being baptized?
note.traditional: verse 37 included: And Philip said, If thou believest with all thine heart, thou mayest. And he answered and said, I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God.

verse.note: Verse 37 is absent from the earliest and best manuscripts and is not printed in the Greek text translated here, so the numbering passes from 36 to 38. In later manuscripts Philip answers, 'If you believe with all your heart, you may,' and the eunuch replies, 'I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God.' The addition was already known in the late second century and probably reflects early baptismal practice, but scholars widely agree it was not part of Luke's text.

verse.text: He ordered the chariot to stop, and they both went down into the water, Philip and the eunuch, and he baptized him.
When they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord snatched Philip away, and the eunuch saw him no more, for he went on his way rejoicing.
Philip, however, turned up at Azotus, and as he passed through he announced the good news to all the cities until he came to Caesarea.
But Saul, still breathing threats and murder against the disciples of the Lord, went to the high priest
and asked him for letters to the synagogues in Damascus, so that if he found any who belonged to the Way, men or women, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem.
verse.note: In Acts ‘the Way’ is a name the early followers of Jesus used for their own movement. The Greek word is the ordinary one for a road or journey, and it is the same word translated ‘road’ in verses 17 and 27, so Saul meets Jesus on the road while hunting people of the Way.

verse.text: As he was on his way and nearing Damascus, suddenly a light from heaven flashed around him,
and falling to the ground he heard a voice saying to him, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?”
He said, “Who are you, Lord?” And he replied, “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.
verse.note: The Greek address can be a respectful ‘sir’ or the title ‘Lord’. Saul does not yet know who is speaking, but he is answering a voice from heaven, so the stronger sense is kept here, as in most translations. Some interpreters prefer ‘sir’ at this point.

text.q: But get up and go into the city, and you will be told what you must do.”

verse.text: The men traveling with him stood speechless, hearing the voice but seeing no one.
verse.note: The Greek word means both ‘voice’ and ‘sound’. In Paul’s own retelling at Acts 22:9 his companions ‘did not hear the voice’ of the one speaking, and many interpreters reconcile the two by taking this verse to mean that they heard a sound without making out words. Whether the grammar itself signals that distinction is disputed.

verse.text: Saul got up from the ground, but though his eyes were open he could see nothing. So they led him by the hand and brought him into Damascus.
For three days he was without sight, and he neither ate nor drank.
Now there was a disciple in Damascus named Ananias, and the Lord said to him in a vision, “Ananias.” He said, “Here I am, Lord.”
The Lord said to him, “Get up and go to the street called Straight, and at the house of Judas look for a man from Tarsus named Saul; for look, he is praying,

text.q: and he has seen in a vision a man named Ananias come in and lay his hands on him so that he may see again.”

verse.text: Ananias answered, “Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much harm he has done to your holy ones in Jerusalem.
verse.note: The traditional rendering is ‘saints’, which many translations keep. The word is used here of all believers as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint’s language for Israel. ‘Saints’ now suggests canonised individuals or people of exceptional virtue. Other translations use ‘God’s people’ or ‘his holy people’.

text.q: And here he has authority from the chief priests to bind all who call on your name.”

verse.text: But the Lord said to him, “Go, for this man is my chosen instrument to carry my name before Gentiles and kings and the children of Israel.
verse.note: The Greek word means ‘peoples’ or ‘nations’, and in the plural it commonly refers to the non-Jewish peoples. This translation renders the one Greek word as ‘Gentiles’ or ‘nations’ according to sense. Here the contrast with ‘the children of Israel’ makes ‘Gentiles’ the natural choice.

text.q: For I myself will show him how much he must suffer for the sake of my name.”

verse.text: So Ananias went and entered the house. Laying his hands on him, he said, “Brother Saul, the Lord has sent me, Jesus who appeared to you on the road as you were coming, so that you may see again and be filled with the Holy Spirit.”
At once something like scales fell from his eyes, and he could see again. He got up and was baptized,
and after taking food he regained his strength. He spent some days with the disciples in Damascus.
At once he began proclaiming in the synagogues that Jesus is the Son of God.

All who heard him were astonished and said, “Isn’t this the man who wreaked havoc in Jerusalem on those who call on this name? And hadn’t he come here for this very purpose, to bring them bound before the chief priests?”
But Saul grew all the more powerful and confounded the Jews living in Damascus, proving that this man is the Messiah.
verse.note: The traditional rendering is ‘the Christ’. Here the word is a title under debate in the synagogues, the anointed king Israel expected, and ‘Messiah’ conveys that to a modern reader. Where the word functions as part of Jesus’s name, as in verse 34, ‘Christ’ is kept. Several modern translations make the same distinction.

verse.text: When many days had passed, the Jews plotted together to kill him,
but their plot became known to Saul. They were even watching the gates day and night in order to kill him,
but his disciples took him by night and let him down through the wall, lowering him in a basket.
verse.note: The earliest manuscripts read ‘his disciples’, meaning people Saul had won over in Damascus. Many later manuscripts read ‘the disciples took him’, which avoids the surprise of Saul already having disciples of his own. Paul mentions the same escape in 2 Corinthians 11:32–33.

verse.text: When he arrived in Jerusalem, he tried to join the disciples, but they were all afraid of him, not believing that he was a disciple.

But Barnabas took him, brought him to the apostles, and described to them how on the road he had seen the Lord, and that the Lord had spoken to him, and how in Damascus he had spoken boldly in the name of Jesus.
So he was with them, going in and out in Jerusalem, speaking boldly in the name of the Lord.
He spoke and debated with the Greek-speaking Jews, but they were trying to kill him.
verse.note: The traditional rendering is ‘Hellenists’ (older versions, ‘Grecians’). The word is rare, and most scholars take it here to mean Jews whose language was Greek, many of them from the diaspora, as distinct from Aramaic-speaking Jews. This is the circle Stephen had argued with in Acts 6. ‘Hellenists’ leaves a modern reader guessing, so the sense is spelled out.

verse.text: When the brothers learned of this, they took him down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus.
So the assembly throughout all Judea and Galilee and Samaria had peace and was being built up; and walking in the fear of the Lord and in the encouragement of the Holy Spirit, it grew in number.
verse.note: The traditional rendering is ‘church’, which is near-universal and which readers readily understand. A first-century hearer knew the word as a civic gathering and as the Septuagint’s term for Israel assembled, whereas ‘church’ now suggests a building or an institution. This translation uses ‘assembly’ throughout so that the one Greek word stays visible. It refers here to the whole community across three regions, not a single meeting.

verse.text: Now as Peter was traveling through all those parts, he came down also to the holy ones living in Lydda.
There he found a man named Aeneas, who had been lying on a mat for eight years, for he was paralyzed.
Peter said to him, “Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you. Get up and make your bed.” And at once he got up.
verse.note: The Greek says only ‘spread for yourself’, with no object. Most take it to mean spreading his own bedding, something a paralyzed man could not do. The same verb is used of preparing a dining couch, so ‘get yourself something to eat’ is also possible.

verse.text: All who lived in Lydda and Sharon saw him, and they turned to the Lord.
Now in Joppa there was a disciple named Tabitha, which translated is Dorcas. She was full of good works and of the acts of charity that she did.
verse.note: Tabitha is Aramaic and Dorcas is Greek; both mean ‘gazelle’. Luke gives his Greek-speaking readers the equivalent name, and she was probably known by both in a mixed port town like Joppa.

verse.text: In those days she became ill and died. They washed her and laid her in an upstairs room.
Since Lydda was near Joppa, the disciples, hearing that Peter was there, sent two men to him with the plea, “Do not delay in coming to us.”

So Peter got up and went with them. When he arrived, they took him up to the upstairs room, and all the widows stood beside him, weeping and showing the tunics and cloaks that Dorcas had made while she was with them.
But Peter sent them all outside, knelt down, and prayed. Then, turning to the body, he said, “Tabitha, get up.” She opened her eyes, and seeing Peter, she sat up.
He gave her his hand and raised her up; then, calling the holy ones and the widows, he presented her alive.
This became known throughout all Joppa, and many believed in the Lord.
And he stayed in Joppa for many days with a certain Simon, a tanner.
verse.note: Tanners worked with animal carcasses and foul-smelling materials, and later Jewish sources treat the trade as disreputable and its practitioners as kept at a distance. Many interpreters think Luke mentions Peter’s host deliberately, as a prelude to the next chapter’s vision about what is clean and unclean. Luke himself does not say so.

verse.text: In Caesarea there was a man named Cornelius, a centurion of the cohort known as the Italian.
He was devout and feared God, as did all his household; he made many charitable gifts to the people and prayed to God continually.
