verse.note: In Acts, 'one who fears God' is close to a set description for Gentiles who worshipped Israel's God and supported the Jewish community without becoming full converts through circumcision. Cornelius is such a person, which is why his gifts go to 'the people', meaning the Jewish people. How formal or fixed this category was is debated.

verse.text: About the ninth hour of the day he saw clearly in a vision an angel of God come in to him and say, “Cornelius!”
verse.note: Hours were counted from sunrise, so the ninth hour is about three in the afternoon and the sixth hour (verse 9) is about noon. The ninth hour was the time of the afternoon sacrifice in the temple and a customary hour of Jewish prayer (see Acts 3:1).

verse.text: He stared at him, terrified, and said, “What is it, Lord?” The angel said to him, “Your prayers and your charitable gifts have gone up as a memorial before God.

text.q: Now send men to Joppa and send for a certain Simon, who is called Peter.
He is lodging with a certain Simon, a tanner, whose house is by the sea.”

verse.text: When the angel who spoke to him had gone, he called two of his household slaves and a devout soldier from among his personal attendants,
and after explaining everything to them, he sent them to Joppa.
The next day, as they were on their way and nearing the city, Peter went up on the roof to pray, about the sixth hour.
He became hungry and wanted something to eat; but while they were preparing it, a trance came over him,
and he saw heaven opened and an object like a large linen sheet coming down, being lowered to the earth by its four corners.
In it were all the four-footed animals and creeping things of the earth and birds of the sky.
And a voice came to him: “Get up, Peter; slaughter and eat.”
But Peter said, “Certainly not, Lord! I have never eaten anything defiled or unclean.”
verse.note: The Greek word ordinarily means 'shared' or 'ordinary', but in Jewish usage it had become a term for what is ritually profane, the opposite of holy; 'common' no longer conveys that. Some scholars distinguish it from 'unclean': unclean animals are those the law forbids, while this word may cover permitted things contaminated by contact with them. Other translations use 'profane' or 'impure'. The related verb in verse 15 is rendered 'call defiled'.

verse.text: And the voice came to him again, a second time: “What God has made clean, you must not call defiled.”
This happened three times, and at once the object was taken up into heaven.
While Peter was at a loss within himself as to what the vision he had seen might mean, just then the men sent by Cornelius, having asked the way to Simon’s house, stood at the gate.
They called out and asked whether Simon who was called Peter was lodging there.
While Peter was still turning the vision over in his mind, the Spirit said to him, “There are men here looking for you.
verse.note: The manuscripts differ here: many read 'three men', one important manuscript reads 'two men', and others give no number. The SBLGNT prints the text without a number, and that is followed here. 'Three' would match the two slaves and one soldier of verse 7.

text.q: Get up now, go down, and go with them without hesitating at all, for I myself have sent them.”

verse.note: The verb can mean 'hesitate, doubt' or 'make a distinction, discriminate'. Most translations take it as hesitation here. Some scholars argue for 'without making any distinction', that is, between Jew and Gentile, which would fit the theme of the chapter and the parallel wording in 11:12.

verse.text: Peter went down to the men and said, “Here I am, the one you are looking for. What is the reason you have come?”

They said, “Cornelius, a centurion, a righteous man who fears God and is well spoken of by the whole nation of the Jews, was directed by a holy angel to send for you to come to his house and to hear what you have to say.”
verse.note: Greek has one word-family where English has two: the same root lies behind 'righteous' and 'just', 'righteousness' and 'justice'. 'Righteous' here and 'righteousness' in verse 35 belong to that single family and describe a person who does what is right before God.

The same Greek word is rendered 'nation' here and in verse 35 and 'Gentiles' in verse 45. In the singular it means a people or nation, Israel included; in the plural it commonly means the non-Jewish peoples.

verse.text: So he invited them in and gave them lodging. The next day he got up and set out with them, and some of the brothers from Joppa went with him.
The day after that he entered Caesarea. Cornelius was expecting them and had called together his relatives and close friends.
As Peter was coming in, Cornelius met him, fell at his feet, and paid him homage.
verse.note: The verb describes bowing or prostrating oneself before a superior, and was used of homage to kings and dignitaries as well as to gods. 'Worshiped' is the traditional rendering, and Peter's reply shows he regarded the gesture as more than a human being should accept. The word itself does not say that Cornelius thought Peter divine.

verse.text: But Peter raised him up, saying, “Stand up. I myself am a human being too.”
Talking with him, he went in and found many people gathered,
and he said to them, “You yourselves know that it is forbidden for a Jewish man to associate with or visit a foreigner. But God has shown me that I should call no person defiled or unclean.
verse.note: The word means contrary to accepted custom or to what is religiously permitted; it is not the usual term for a breach of the written law. No command in the Torah forbids associating with Gentiles. Peter is describing a widely held purity practice, concerned especially with Gentile homes and food, and Jewish practice in fact varied. Most translations have 'unlawful' or 'against our law'.

text.q: That is why I came without objection when I was sent for. So I ask, for what reason did you send for me?”

verse.text: And Cornelius said, “Four days ago at this very hour, the ninth, I was praying in my house, when a man in shining clothing stood before me

note.term: Four days ago at this very hour
note.traditional: Four days ago, about this hour

verse.note: The Greek is awkward, literally 'from the fourth day until this hour I was praying the ninth hour', and its exact sense is uncertain. Most translations take it as given here; counting inclusively, this is the fourth day since the vision. Many later manuscripts add that Cornelius was fasting.

text.q: and said, ‘Cornelius, your prayer has been heard and your charitable gifts have been remembered before God.
So send to Joppa and summon Simon, who is called Peter. He is lodging in the house of Simon, a tanner, by the sea.’
So I sent to you at once, and it was good of you to come. Now then, we are all here in the presence of God to hear everything the Lord has commanded you.”

verse.text: Then Peter opened his mouth and said, “In truth I am coming to see that God shows no favoritism,

text.q: but in every nation the one who fears him and practices righteousness is acceptable to him.
As for the message he sent to the sons of Israel, announcing the good news of peace through Jesus Christ—he is Lord of all—

verse.note: The Greek of verses 36 to 38 is grammatically broken: 'the message' is left hanging and there is no main verb until 'you know' in verse 37. Some translations supply 'You know the message' in verse 36. Others follow manuscripts that omit the relative pronoun and read 'He sent the message to the sons of Israel'. The rendering here keeps the loose construction.

text.q: you yourselves know what took place throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee after the baptism that John proclaimed:
how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power, and how he went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, because God was with him.
And we are witnesses of everything he did both in the country of the Jews and in Jerusalem. They put him to death by hanging him on a tree,

verse.note: The traditional 'tree' is kept because the phrase echoes Deuteronomy 21:22–23, where the body of an executed criminal hung up in public is said to be under God's curse. A Jewish hearer would have caught that echo. The Greek word covers wood and anything made of it, including a post or gallows, and here refers to the cross.

text.q: but God raised him on the third day and granted that he be plainly seen,
not by all the people but by witnesses God had chosen beforehand, by us, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead.
He ordered us to proclaim to the people and to testify solemnly that he is the one appointed by God as judge of the living and the dead.
To him all the prophets bear witness, that everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name.”

verse.text: While Peter was still speaking these words, the Holy Spirit fell on all who were listening to the message.
The circumcised believers who had come with Peter were astounded that the gift of the Holy Spirit had been poured out on the Gentiles too,
for they heard them speaking in tongues and extolling God. Then Peter responded,

text.q: “Surely no one can withhold the water and keep these people from being baptized, who have received the Holy Spirit just as we did?”

verse.text: And he commanded that they be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Then they asked him to stay on for some days.
Now the apostles and the brothers and sisters throughout Judea heard that the Gentiles too had received the word of God.
verse.note: The Greek word means 'peoples' or 'nations'. In the plural, in Jewish usage, it means the non-Jewish peoples. This translation uses 'Gentiles' for that sense and 'nations' where peoples as such are meant, but it is one Greek word throughout.

The masculine plural was the ordinary Greek way to address or describe a mixed group of siblings, and here it means the members of the community, women included. Older translations have 'brethren' or 'brothers', and several modern ones have 'brothers and sisters' or 'believers'. In verse 12, where six particular men are meant, 'brothers' is kept.

verse.text: But when Peter went up to Jerusalem, those of the circumcision took issue with him,

note.traditional: they that were of the circumcision / the circumcision party

verse.note: The phrase can simply mean Jewish believers, which at this point is nearly everyone in the Jerusalem community. It can also mean a group within it that held strictly to circumcision. Some translations decide for the second with 'the circumcision party', but the Greek does not settle it and the rendering here leaves it open.

verse.text: saying, “You went in to uncircumcised men and ate with them!”
verse.note: The Greek is blunt: literally 'men having a foreskin'. The charge is not that Peter preached to Gentiles but that he entered their home and shared their table. Many observant Jews avoided this because Gentile food and households were regarded as sources of impurity.

verse.text: But Peter began and set it out for them in order, saying:

text.q: “I was in the city of Joppa praying, and in a trance I saw a vision: an object coming down, like a great linen sheet being lowered from heaven by its four corners, and it came right up to me.
I stared into it and looked closely, and I saw the four-footed animals of the earth, the wild beasts, the crawling things, and the birds of the sky.
I also heard a voice saying to me, ‘Get up, Peter; slaughter and eat.’
But I said, ‘Certainly not, Lord! Nothing profane or unclean has ever entered my mouth.’

verse.note: The word ordinarily means 'shared, common'. In Jewish Greek it had become a term for what is ritually ordinary as opposed to holy, and so unfit for a Jew to eat. 'Common' is the traditional rendering, but a modern reader hears it as 'frequent' or 'ordinary'. 'Profane' is used here in its older sense of 'not holy', and the related verb in verse 9 is rendered 'call profane' to keep the echo.

text.q: But a voice from heaven answered a second time, ‘What God has made clean, you must not call profane.’
This happened three times, and then everything was drawn up again into heaven.
And at that very moment three men arrived at the house where we were, sent to me from Caesarea.
The Spirit told me to go with them, making no distinction. These six brothers also came with me, and we went into the man’s house.

verse.note: The verb can mean 'to make a distinction' or, mostly in the middle voice, 'to hesitate, to doubt'. The form here is active, which favors 'making no distinction' between Jew and Gentile. Older translations render 'without hesitating', as in the parallel at 10:20. The same verb is used in verse 2 for the critics 'taking issue' with Peter, which may be a deliberate echo.

text.q: He told us how he had seen the angel standing in his house and saying,
‘Send to Joppa and summon Simon, who is called Peter;
he will speak words to you by which you will be saved, you and all your household.’
As I began to speak, the Holy Spirit fell on them, just as on us at the beginning.
And I remembered the word of the Lord, how he used to say,
‘John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.’
So if God gave them the same gift he gave us when we believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I to be able to hinder God?”

verse.text: When they heard this, they fell silent and glorified God, saying, “So then, God has granted even the Gentiles the turning back that leads to life.”
verse.note: The traditional rendering is 'repentance', which most translations keep as an established term. In modern English it centres on feeling sorry. The Greek word, shaped by the prophets' call to 'return' to God, means a change of direction in mind and conduct, and 'turning back' is used for it throughout this translation.

verse.text: Now those who had been scattered by the trouble that arose over Stephen traveled as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus, and Antioch, speaking the word to no one except Jews.
verse.note: Most translations have 'persecution' here, which describes the events of chapter 8 accurately. The Greek word is the general one for distress or affliction, not the specific word for persecution used at 8:1. The plainer rendering keeps the two apart.

verse.text: But some of them were men of Cyprus and Cyrene, who came to Antioch and began speaking to the Greek-speakers as well, proclaiming the good news of the Lord Jesus.
verse.note: Manuscripts are divided between 'Hellenists' (Greek-speakers), the reading translated here, and 'Greeks'. At Acts 6:1 the first word means Greek-speaking Jews. Here the contrast with 'Jews' in verse 19 shows that non-Jews are meant, whichever reading is original. Many translations therefore print 'Greeks'.

verse.text: The hand of the Lord was with them, and a great number who believed turned to the Lord.
The report about them reached the ears of the assembly in Jerusalem, and they sent Barnabas out as far as Antioch.
verse.note: The traditional rendering is 'church', which is near-universal and which readers readily understand. A first-century hearer knew the word as a civic gathering and as the Septuagint's term for Israel assembled, whereas 'church' now suggests a building or an institution. This translation uses 'assembly' wherever the word occurs, though it can sound like a single meeting and not a standing community.

verse.text: When he arrived and saw the grace of God, he was glad, and he encouraged them all to stay with the Lord with resolute hearts,
for he was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith. And a sizeable crowd was added to the Lord.
Then he went off to Tarsus to look for Saul,

and when he found him he brought him to Antioch. And so for a whole year they met together with the assembly and taught a sizeable crowd, and it was in Antioch that the disciples were first called Christians.
verse.note: The word is formed with a Latin-style ending used for the adherents or partisans of a leader, so it means roughly 'Christ's people'. It appears only three times in the New Testament and is not a name believers use for themselves there. Many scholars think outsiders in Antioch coined it, though this is not certain. The verb can mean either 'were called' or 'took the name'.

verse.text: In those days prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch.
One of them, named Agabus, stood up and indicated through the Spirit that there was going to be a great famine over the whole inhabited world. This took place under Claudius.
verse.note: The word means the inhabited world, and in common usage often amounted to the Roman empire. Claudius was emperor from AD 41 to 54. Ancient sources mention food shortages in several regions during his reign, including a severe famine in Judea in the mid-40s. No single empire-wide famine is recorded, so the phrase is probably a general expression for widespread scarcity.

verse.text: The disciples decided that each of them, according to their means, would send aid to the brothers and sisters living in Judea.
This they did, sending it to the elders by the hand of Barnabas and Saul.
About that time King Herod laid hands on some who belonged to the assembly, to do them harm.
verse.note: The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering and the Septuagint's word for Israel assembled before God. 'Church' is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution, which the word did not. 'Assembly' is used throughout this translation so that the one Greek word appears as one English word.

This is Herod Agrippa I, grandson of Herod the Great, who ruled Judea as king from AD 41 to 44. He is a different man from the Herod of Jesus's birth and from Herod Antipas, who appears in the accounts of Jesus's trial.

verse.text: He had James, the brother of John, killed with the sword.
Seeing that this pleased the Jews, he went on to arrest Peter as well. This was during the days of Unleavened Bread.
After seizing him, he put him in prison and handed him over to four squads of four soldiers to guard him, intending to bring him out before the people after the Passover.
verse.note: Passover was followed immediately by the seven days of Unleavened Bread, and by this period either name could be used for the whole festival. 'After the Passover' here means after the festival week mentioned in verse 3 had ended. The King James Version's 'Easter' in this verse is an anachronism.
The night was divided into four watches, so four squads allowed a fresh team of four for each watch. Verse 6 shows the arrangement: two soldiers chained to the prisoner and two on guard at the door.

verse.text: So Peter was kept in the prison, but prayer for him was being earnestly made to God by the assembly.
When Herod was about to bring him out, that very night Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains, while guards in front of the door kept watch over the prison.
Suddenly an angel of the Lord stood there, and a light shone in the cell. He struck Peter on the side and woke him, saying, “Get up quickly!” And the chains fell from his hands.
The angel said to him, “Fasten your belt and put on your sandals.” He did so. Then the angel said to him, “Wrap your cloak around you and follow me.”
He went out and followed, not knowing that what was happening through the angel was real; he thought he was seeing a vision.

They passed the first guard post and the second and came to the iron gate that leads into the city, which opened for them by itself. They went out and walked the length of one street, and at once the angel left him.
Then Peter came to himself and said, “Now I truly know that the Lord sent his angel and rescued me from Herod’s hand and from everything the people of the Jews were expecting.”
When he had taken this in, he went to the house of Mary, the mother of John who was also called Mark, where a good number had gathered and were praying.
When he knocked at the door of the gateway, a slave girl named Rhoda came to answer.
verse.note: In the Greek of this period the word normally meant a female slave, and that is how a first-century reader would have taken it. Most English versions soften it to 'servant girl' or 'maid', which suggests a hired employee. Rhoda was most likely a slave of Mary's household, and evidently one of the believers.

verse.text: Recognizing Peter’s voice, in her joy she did not open the gateway but ran in and told them that Peter was standing at the gateway.
They said to her, “You are out of your mind!” But she kept insisting that it was so. They said, “It is his angel.”
verse.note: The speakers seem to assume that a person has an angel who watches over them and may look or sound like them; a similar idea lies behind Matthew 18:10. Some interpreters think they mean that Peter has been killed and this is his spirit, but the word used is the normal one for an angel.

verse.text: But Peter kept on knocking, and when they opened they saw him and were astounded.

Motioning to them with his hand to be quiet, he described to them how the Lord had brought him out of the prison. And he said, “Tell this to James and the brothers and sisters.” Then he went out and travelled to another place.
verse.note: This is not James the brother of John, whose death was reported in verse 2. It is James the brother of Jesus, who by this time was a leading figure in the Jerusalem community (see Acts 15 and Galatians 1:19).

The Greek masculine plural was the ordinary way of referring to a mixed group of siblings, and here it means the members of the community, women included. Traditional versions have 'the brothers' or 'the brethren'. A minority of interpreters think a narrower group of leaders is meant.

verse.text: When day came, there was no small commotion among the soldiers over what had become of Peter.
Herod searched for him and did not find him; he interrogated the guards and ordered them led away to execution. Then he went down from Judea to Caesarea and stayed there.
verse.note: The Greek says only that he ordered them 'led away'. The verb was a common legal term for taking someone off to punishment, especially execution, and most translators understand it so here; a guard who lost a prisoner could be made to bear the prisoner's penalty. It could mean simply that they were taken into custody.

verse.text: Now Herod was furious with the people of Tyre and Sidon. They came to him together, and after winning over Blastus, the king’s chamberlain, they asked for peace, because their country drew its food from the king’s.
On an appointed day Herod put on royal robes, took his seat on the platform, and began delivering a public address to them.
verse.note: The Greek word denotes a raised platform from which an official addressed the public or heard legal cases. It is not the word for a royal throne. Many versions have 'throne' here; others have 'tribunal', 'rostrum' or 'judgment seat'.

verse.text: The crowd kept shouting, “The voice of a god, not of a human being!”
Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him, because he did not give the glory to God, and he was eaten by worms and breathed his last.
verse.note: The Jewish historian Josephus gives an independent account of Agrippa's death in AD 44 (Antiquities, book 19). At a festival in Caesarea, the crowd hailed him as a god while he wore a dazzling robe; he did not rebuke them, was seized with violent abdominal pain, and died some days later. The verb 'struck' is the same one used of the angel waking Peter in verse 7: one blow rescues, the other destroys.

verse.text: But the word of God grew and multiplied.
Barnabas and Saul returned, having completed their service in Jerusalem, and they took along with them John, who was called Mark.

note.term: having completed their service in Jerusalem

verse.note: The earliest manuscripts read 'to Jerusalem', which is difficult because Barnabas and Saul were already there (11:30) and next appear in Antioch (13:1). Other manuscripts read 'from Jerusalem', probably a correction, and many English versions follow them. The edition translated here keeps 'to Jerusalem' and punctuates so that the phrase goes with 'their service' rather than with 'returned'; this translation follows it. The service is the famine relief of 11:29–30.

verse.text: Now in Antioch, in the assembly there, there were prophets and teachers: Barnabas, Simeon who was called Niger, Lucius the Cyrenian, Manaen who had been brought up with Herod the tetrarch, and Saul.
verse.note: The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering and the Septuagint's word for Israel assembled before God. 'Church' is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. 'Assembly' is used throughout this translation so that the reader can see it is one Greek word.

verse.text: While they were worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, “Now set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.”
Then, after fasting and praying, they laid their hands on them and sent them off.
So, sent out by the Holy Spirit, they went down to Seleucia, and from there they sailed to Cyprus.
When they arrived in Salamis, they proclaimed the word of God in the synagogues of the Jews. They also had John as their assistant.
After traveling through the whole island as far as Paphos, they came upon a certain magician, a Jewish false prophet named Bar-Jesus,
who was with the proconsul Sergius Paulus, an intelligent man. The proconsul summoned Barnabas and Saul and sought to hear the word of God.
But Elymas the magician—for that is how his name is translated—opposed them, seeking to turn the proconsul away from the faith.
But Saul, who is also called Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, looked intently at him
and said, “You who are full of every kind of deceit and every kind of fraud, you son of the devil, you enemy of all righteousness, will you not stop twisting the straight paths of the Lord?
verse.note: Greek has one word-family where English has two: righteous and just, righteousness and justice, and the verb 'justify' are all the same root. The verb rendered 'justified' in verses 38–39 belongs to this family and means being declared or put in the right. Some scholars prefer 'justice' for the noun, as translations into most other languages do.

verse.text: And now, look, the hand of the Lord is upon you, and you will be blind, not seeing the sun for a time.” Immediately mist and darkness fell on him, and he went about looking for people to lead him by the hand.
Then the proconsul, seeing what had happened, believed, astounded at the teaching of the Lord.
Paul and his companions put out to sea from Paphos and came to Perga in Pamphylia. But John left them and returned to Jerusalem.
They themselves went on from Perga and arrived at Pisidian Antioch, and on the Sabbath day they went into the synagogue and sat down.
After the reading of the Law and the Prophets, the synagogue leaders sent word to them, saying, “Brothers, if you have any word of encouragement for the people, speak.”
Paul stood up, motioned with his hand, and said, “Israelites, and you who fear God, listen.
verse.note: Paul addresses two groups: Israelites by birth, and non-Jews who attended the synagogue and honored Israel's God, some of them without becoming full converts. The 'devout' proselytes and women of verses 43 and 50 are described with a related term for worshipers attached to the synagogue. How fixed a category 'God-fearers' was is debated.

text.q: The God of this people Israel chose our fathers, and he lifted the people up while they lived as foreigners in the land of Egypt, and with an uplifted arm he led them out of it.
For about forty years he put up with them in the wilderness.

note.traditional: suffered he their manners / put up with them

verse.note: Manuscripts are divided between two verbs that differ by a single letter: 'put up with their ways' and 'carried them as a nurse carries a child', that is, 'cared for them'. The same variation appears in the Greek text of Deuteronomy 1:31, which Paul is echoing. The SBLGNT reads the first; the evidence is closely balanced.

text.q: And after overthrowing seven nations in the land of Canaan, he gave their land as an inheritance.

verse.note: The same Greek word is rendered 'Gentiles' in verses 46–48. It means a people or nation, and in the plural it often means the non-Jewish peoples as a group. This translation chooses between the two English words by sense, as is standard practice.

text.q: All this took about four hundred and fifty years. After that he gave them judges until Samuel the prophet.

note.term: All this took about four hundred and fifty years
note.traditional: after that he gave unto them judges about the space of four hundred and fifty years

verse.note: The Greek is simply 'for about four hundred and fifty years', and here it closes the preceding sentence, so the figure covers the time in Egypt, the wilderness and the conquest. Later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, place the phrase after 'after this', making it the length of the period of the judges. The earliest manuscripts support the order translated here.

text.q: Then they asked for a king, and God gave them Saul son of Kish, a man from the tribe of Benjamin, for forty years.
After removing him, he raised up David to be their king, and of him he testified, ‘I have found David son of Jesse, a man after my own heart, who will carry out all my wishes.’
From this man’s offspring God, as he promised, has brought to Israel a savior, Jesus.
Before his arrival, John had proclaimed a baptism of turning back to all the people of Israel.

verse.note: The traditional 'repentance' now centers on feeling sorry. The Greek word, in Jewish usage, carries the prophets' call to return to God: a change of direction in mind and conduct. Most translations keep 'repentance' as an established term understood to include a change of life.

text.q: And as John was completing his course, he used to say, ‘What do you suppose I am? I am not he. But look, after me comes one whose sandals I am not worthy to untie from his feet.’
Brothers, sons of Abraham’s family and those among you who fear God, it is to us that the word of this salvation has been sent.
For the people living in Jerusalem and their rulers did not recognize him, and by condemning him they fulfilled the voices of the prophets that are read every Sabbath.
Though they found no ground for a death sentence, they asked Pilate to have him put to death.
When they had carried out everything that was written about him, they took him down from the tree and laid him in a tomb.
But God raised him from the dead,
and for many days he appeared to those who had come up with him from Galilee to Jerusalem, who are now his witnesses to the people.
And we bring you the good news about the promise made to the fathers:
God has fulfilled it for our children by raising up Jesus, as it is also written in the second psalm: ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you.’

verse.note: The earliest manuscripts read 'for our children', which the SBLGNT prints and which is translated here. Many scholars suspect an early copying error, since the sense expected is 'for us, their children', the reading found in later manuscripts and followed by most English versions. The question remains open.

note.traditional: in that he hath raised up Jesus again

verse.note: The verb can mean raising someone from the dead or bringing someone onto the stage of history, as God 'raised up' David in verse 22. Most interpreters take it here of the resurrection, in view of verses 30 and 34; others think Jesus' appearance in Israel is meant, with the resurrection first addressed in verse 34. The translation leaves both possible.

text.q: And as for his raising him from the dead, never again to return to decay, he has spoken in this way: ‘I will give you the holy and faithful things of David.’

note.term: the holy and faithful things of David

verse.note: This quotes the Greek version of Isaiah 55:3, where the phrase refers to the lasting covenant blessings promised to David. The word 'holy' here is the same word as 'Holy One' in the next verse, quoted from Psalm 16, and the argument depends on that link. Many translations render 'the holy and sure blessings of David', which obscures the connection less than the older 'sure mercies'.

text.q: That is why he also says in another psalm, ‘You will not let your Holy One see decay.’
For David, after serving God’s purpose in his own generation, fell asleep, was gathered to his fathers, and saw decay,
but the one whom God raised did not see decay.
So let it be known to you, brothers, that through this man forgiveness of sins is being proclaimed to you, and from everything from which you could not be justified by the law of Moses,
by this man everyone who believes is justified.
So watch out that what is said in the Prophets does not come upon you:
‘Look, you scoffers, be amazed and perish, for I am doing a work in your days, a work you will never believe, even if someone describes it to you.’”

verse.text: As they were leaving, the people urged that these words be spoken to them on the next Sabbath.
When the synagogue meeting had broken up, many of the Jews and of the devout proselytes followed Paul and Barnabas, who spoke with them and urged them to remain in the grace of God.
On the following Sabbath almost the whole city gathered to hear the word of the Lord.
But when the Jews saw the crowds, they were filled with jealousy, and they contradicted what Paul was saying, speaking abusively.

Paul and Barnabas spoke out boldly and said, “It was necessary that the word of God be spoken to you first. Since you push it away and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, look, we are turning to the Gentiles.
verse.note: The adjective comes from the word for 'age'. In Jewish usage 'eternal life' is the life of the age to come, a matter of its kind as well as its unending length. A minority of translators render 'life of the age to come' throughout.

text.q: For this is what the Lord has commanded us: ‘I have set you as a light for the Gentiles, so that you may bring salvation to the end of the earth.’”

verse.text: When the Gentiles heard this, they rejoiced and glorified the word of the Lord, and all who were appointed to eternal life believed.
verse.note: The verb means to assign or set in place, and the passive is usually understood to mean that God had appointed these people to eternal life. Some interpreters read the form as a middle voice, 'had set themselves toward' or 'were disposed to' eternal life, in contrast with those in verse 46 who judged themselves unworthy of it. The passive reading is the majority view and is followed here.

verse.text: And the word of the Lord spread through the whole region.
But the Jews stirred up the devout women of high standing and the leading men of the city, roused persecution against Paul and Barnabas, and drove them out of their territory.
But they shook the dust off their feet against them and went to Iconium.
And the disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit.
In Iconium the same thing happened: they went into the synagogue of the Jews and spoke in such a way that a great number of both Jews and Greeks believed.

note.traditional: they went both together into the synagogue

verse.note: The Greek phrase kata to auto can mean either "in the same way" (as at Pisidian Antioch in the previous chapter) or "together." Older versions and some modern ones take it as "together"; many recent translations take it as "in the same way" or "as usual." The rendering here follows the second reading, which fits the repeated pattern of synagogue preaching, a divided response and expulsion.

verse.text: But the Jews who refused to believe stirred up the Gentiles and embittered their souls against the brothers.
verse.note: A single Greek word, ethnē, lies behind both "Gentiles" (verses 2, 5, 27) and "nations" (verse 16). In Jewish usage the plural meant the non-Jewish peoples. It is rendered "nations" where the peoples of the world as a whole are in view, and "Gentiles" where non-Jews are contrasted with Jews.

verse.text: So they stayed a considerable time, speaking boldly in reliance on the Lord, who bore witness to the word of his grace by granting signs and wonders to be done through their hands.
But the people of the city were divided: some were with the Jews and some with the apostles.
verse.note: Only here and in verse 14 does Acts call Paul and Barnabas "apostles"; elsewhere in the book the term is kept for the Twelve. The word means an authorised envoy. Many scholars think it is used here of the two as emissaries sent out by the assembly at Antioch (13:1-3).

verse.text: When a move was made by both Gentiles and Jews, together with their leaders, to abuse them and stone them,
they learned of it and fled to the cities of Lycaonia, Lystra and Derbe, and to the surrounding region,
and there they went on proclaiming the good news.
In Lystra there sat a man who had no use of his feet, lame from his mother’s womb, who had never walked.
This man listened to Paul speaking. Paul looked straight at him and, seeing that he had faith to be made well,
verse.note: The Greek verb covers both physical rescue or healing and salvation in the fuller religious sense. Here the immediate meaning is healing. Luke often lets the wider sense sound alongside it, and some translators render it "to be saved."

verse.text: said in a loud voice, “Stand up straight on your feet!” And he sprang up and began to walk.
When the crowds saw what Paul had done, they raised their voices and said in Lycaonian, “The gods have become like human beings and come down to us!”
They called Barnabas Zeus, and Paul Hermes, because he was the one who took the lead in speaking.
verse.note: Zeus was the chief of the Greek gods and Hermes was the gods' messenger and spokesman, which is why Paul, the speaker, is identified as Hermes. A legend told by the Roman poet Ovid has Zeus and Hermes visiting this general region in human disguise and being refused hospitality by all but one elderly couple. Such a story may explain the crowd's eagerness not to repeat the mistake.

verse.text: The priest of Zeus, whose temple stood just outside the city, brought bulls and garlands to the gates and wanted to offer sacrifice together with the crowds.
verse.note: The Greek does not say which gates are meant. They may be the city gates, the gates of the temple precinct outside the city, or the gateway of the house where Paul and Barnabas were staying. The Greek speaks literally of "the Zeus who is before the city," a way of naming the god by his shrine's location; "whose temple stood" makes that explicit.

verse.text: But when the apostles Barnabas and Paul heard of it, they tore their clothes and rushed out into the crowd, shouting,

text.q: “Men, why are you doing this? We too are human beings, of the same nature as you, bringing you the good news that you should turn from these worthless things to a living God, who made the heaven and the earth and the sea and everything in them.

verse.note: In the Greek Old Testament this word ("empty, futile") is a regular term for idols and the gods they represent. The apostles are speaking of the gods the crowd is about to sacrifice to. The description of God that follows, maker of heaven, earth, sea and everything in them, echoes Exodus 20:11 and Psalm 146:6.

text.q: In past generations he let all the nations go their own ways;
yet he did not leave himself without witness: he did good, giving you rains from heaven and fruitful seasons, filling your hearts with food and gladness.”

verse.text: Even with these words they barely stopped the crowds from sacrificing to them.
But Jews came from Antioch and Iconium and won over the crowds. They stoned Paul and dragged him outside the city, supposing that he was dead.
But when the disciples gathered around him, he got up and went into the city. The next day he left with Barnabas for Derbe.
After they had proclaimed the good news to that city and made a considerable number of disciples, they returned to Lystra, to Iconium, and to Antioch,
strengthening the souls of the disciples and urging them to continue in the faith, saying, “It is through many hardships that we must enter the kingdom of God.”
After appointing elders for them in each assembly, with prayer and fasting they entrusted them to the Lord in whom they had come to believe.
verse.note: The verb originally described voting by a show of hands, and some interpreters argue that the congregations elected their elders. By this period it was widely used simply for "appoint," and the grammar here makes Paul and Barnabas the ones who do it. "Ordained" in older versions imports a later church rite.

The traditional rendering is "church," which is near-universal and which readers understand. A first-century hearer, however, knew this word as the ordinary term for a civic gathering and as the Greek Old Testament's word for Israel assembled, whereas "church" now suggests a building or an institution. "Assembly" is used throughout this translation so that the reader can see it is one Greek word; it means the community of believers in a place, not a single meeting.

verse.text: Then they passed through Pisidia and came to Pamphylia,
and after speaking the word in Perga they went down to Attalia.
From there they sailed to Antioch, where they had been committed to the grace of God for the work they had now completed.
verse.note: Two different cities are called Antioch in this chapter. In verses 19 and 21 it is Antioch near Pisidia in central Asia Minor, where Paul preached in chapter 13. Here it is the great city of Antioch in Syria, whose assembly had sent Paul and Barnabas out (13:1-3) and to which they now report back.

verse.text: When they arrived, they gathered the assembly together and reported all that God had done with them, and that he had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles.
And they stayed no short time with the disciples.
Then some men came down from Judea and began teaching the brothers, “Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved.”
verse.note: The Greek plural was the ordinary term for fellow members of the community and could include women. Many recent translations render it 'brothers and sisters' or 'believers'. 'Brothers' is kept here throughout the chapter, partly because the letter in verse 23 plays on the word: the Jerusalem leaders write as brothers to brothers.

verse.text: When Paul and Barnabas had no small dissension and debate with them, they appointed Paul and Barnabas and some others of their number to go up to the apostles and elders in Jerusalem about this question.
So, sent on their way by the assembly, they passed through both Phoenicia and Samaria, recounting in detail the conversion of the Gentiles, and they brought great joy to all the brothers.
verse.note: The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering and the Septuagint's term for Israel assembled before God. 'Church' is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. This translation uses 'assembly' everywhere so that the reader can see it is one Greek word; the cost is that it can sound like a single meeting rather than a standing community.

The Greek word means 'peoples' or 'nations', and in the plural it was the standard Jewish term for the non-Jewish peoples. It is the same word throughout this chapter, including 'all the Gentiles' in the quotation at verse 17, where some translations have 'all the nations'.

verse.text: When they arrived in Jerusalem, they were welcomed by the assembly and the apostles and the elders, and they reported all that God had done with them.
But some from the party of the Pharisees who had believed stood up and said, “It is necessary to circumcise them and to command them to keep the law of Moses.”
The apostles and the elders gathered to look into this matter.

After much debate, Peter stood up and said to them, “Brothers, you know well that from the early days God made a choice among you, that through my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the good news and believe.

text.q: And God, who knows the heart, testified to them by giving them the Holy Spirit, just as he did to us,
and he made no distinction between us and them, cleansing their hearts by faith.
So now why are you putting God to the test by placing on the neck of the disciples a yoke that neither our ancestors nor we have been able to bear?
On the contrary, we believe that it is through the grace of the Lord Jesus that we are saved, in the same way as they are.”

verse.note: The Greek infinitive does not specify a time. Most translations render 'we believe that we will be saved'; 'that we are saved' and 'that we were saved' are equally possible. In any reading the emphasis falls on 'through the grace of the Lord Jesus', which stands first in the Greek sentence.

verse.text: The whole company fell silent, and they listened to Barnabas and Paul as they related all the signs and wonders God had done among the Gentiles through them.
When they had fallen silent, James replied, “Brothers, listen to me.

text.q: Simeon has related how God first intervened to take from among the Gentiles a people for his name.

verse.note: Simeon is the Semitic form of the name Simon, and James uses it here for Peter, whose speech he is summarising. A few interpreters have proposed a different Simeon, but most scholars take the reference to Peter as secure.

In the Septuagint this verb is used of God turning his attention to people in order to act for them, and that is the sense here. 'Visited' is the traditional rendering, but in modern English it suggests a social call; some translations have 'looked favourably on' or 'showed his concern'. The same verb in verse 36 has its everyday sense and is translated 'visit'.

'People' translates the Septuagint's regular word for Israel as God's own people, normally set over against 'the Gentiles'. A Jewish hearer would have felt the force of the combination: a people of God drawn from the very nations from which Israel was distinguished.

text.q: And the words of the prophets agree with this, as it is written:
‘After this I will return and rebuild the fallen tent of David; I will rebuild its ruins and set it upright again,

verse.note: The quotation is Amos 9:11–12 in a form close to the Septuagint, with the opening and closing phrases worded differently from Amos. The Greek version differs from the Hebrew, which speaks of Israel possessing 'the remnant of Edom'. The Greek has 'the rest of humanity' seeking the Lord, and it is this form that serves James's argument.

text.q: so that the rest of humanity may seek the Lord, and all the Gentiles over whom my name has been called, says the Lord, who makes these things
known from long ago.’

note.traditional: Known unto God are all his works from the beginning of the world

verse.note: Later manuscripts expand these words into a separate sentence, 'Known to God from of old are all his works', which is the form found in the King James Version. The shorter text followed here is the earliest attested. It can also be construed 'who does these things, which have been known from long ago'; the phrase is not part of Amos and may echo Isaiah 45:21.

text.q: Therefore my judgment is that we should not make trouble for those from the Gentiles who are turning to God,
but should write to them to abstain from things polluted by idols, from sexual immorality, from what has been strangled, and from blood.

verse.note: This refers to meat from animals killed without the blood being drained. The four prohibitions resemble rules that Leviticus 17–18 applies to foreigners living among Israel, and many scholars think that is their source, though this is disputed. One strand of the manuscript tradition (the 'Western' text) omits 'what has been strangled' and adds a negative form of the Golden Rule, which turns the list into a moral code.

text.q: For from ancient generations Moses has had in every city those who proclaim him, since he is read aloud in the synagogues every Sabbath.”

verse.text: Then the apostles and the elders, together with the whole assembly, resolved to choose men from among themselves and send them to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas: Judas called Barsabbas, and Silas, leading men among the brothers.
verse.note: The Greek expression, literally 'it seemed good to', is the standard formula of Greek civic decrees for recording a formal decision ('it was resolved by the council and the people'). The traditional 'it seemed good' is literal, but in modern English it sounds tentative, which the formula is not. The same expression recurs in verses 25 and 28, where the familiar wording is 'it seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us'.

verse.text: They wrote this letter to be delivered by them: “The apostles and the elders, your brothers, to the brothers from among the Gentiles in Antioch, Syria and Cilicia: greetings.

text.q: Since we have heard that some who went out from among us have disturbed you with their words and unsettled your minds, though we gave them no such instructions,
we have resolved, having come to one mind, to choose men and send them to you with our beloved Barnabas and Paul,
people who have risked their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.

verse.note: The Greek says literally that they have 'handed over their lives'. Most translations take this as 'risked their lives', which is followed here. It can also mean 'devoted their lives', and some interpreters prefer that.

text.q: So we have sent Judas and Silas, who will themselves report the same things by word of mouth.
For the Holy Spirit and we have resolved to lay no further burden on you beyond these necessary things:
to abstain from what has been sacrificed to idols, from blood, from what has been strangled, and from sexual immorality. If you keep yourselves from these, you will do well. Farewell.”

verse.text: So they were sent off and went down to Antioch, and after gathering the company together they delivered the letter.
When they read it, they rejoiced at the encouragement.
Judas and Silas, who were themselves prophets, encouraged the brothers at length and strengthened them.
After spending some time there, they were sent off in peace by the brothers to those who had sent them.

note.term: to those who had sent them

verse.note: Verse 34 ('But it seemed good to Silas to remain there') is absent from the earliest manuscripts and from the Greek text translated here, so the numbering passes from 33 to 35. It was probably added by a copyist to explain how Silas comes to be in Antioch at verse 40.

verse.text: But Paul and Barnabas stayed on in Antioch, teaching and proclaiming the good news of the word of the Lord, together with many others.
After some days Paul said to Barnabas, “Let us go back and visit the brothers in every city where we proclaimed the word of the Lord, and see how they are doing.”
Barnabas wanted to take along John called Mark as well.
But Paul held that they should not take along this man, who had deserted them in Pamphylia and had not gone on with them to the work.
The disagreement became so sharp that they parted from each other; Barnabas took Mark and sailed away to Cyprus,
while Paul chose Silas and set out, entrusted by the brothers to the grace of the Lord.
He passed through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the assemblies.
He also came to Derbe and to Lystra. A disciple was there named Timothy, the son of a believing Jewish woman but of a Greek father,
who was well spoken of by the brothers and sisters in Lystra and Iconium.
verse.note: The Greek plural was the ordinary way to address or describe a mixed group of men and women, and here it means the members of the community in general. In verse 40 the group meets in Lydia’s house and plainly includes her. Older translations have “brethren” or “brothers”; many recent ones render it as here.

verse.text: Paul wanted this man to go out with him, and he took him and circumcised him because of the Jews who were in those places, for they all knew that his father was a Greek.
As they traveled through the cities, they handed on to them the decrees decided on by the apostles and elders in Jerusalem, to be kept.
So the assemblies were being strengthened in the faith and were growing in number day by day.
verse.note: The Greek word meant a gathering of people, used both for a city’s civic assembly and, in the Greek Old Testament, for Israel gathered before God. “Church” is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. This translation uses “assembly” throughout so that the reader can see it is one Greek word.

verse.text: They went through the Phrygian and Galatian region, having been prevented by the Holy Spirit from speaking the word in Asia.

note.traditional: the region of Phrygia and Galatia

verse.note: The Greek can mean one region that was both Phrygian and Galatian (the part of Phrygia inside the Roman province of Galatia) or two regions, Phrygia and then the Galatian territory further north. The choice bears on the long-running debate over which communities Paul’s letter to the Galatians was written to. Scholars remain divided.
This is the Roman province of Asia, the western part of modern Turkey with Ephesus as its chief city, not the continent.

verse.text: When they came up to Mysia, they tried to go on into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus did not let them.
So, passing by Mysia, they went down to Troas.
And a vision appeared to Paul during the night: a Macedonian man was standing there, appealing to him and saying, “Cross over to Macedonia and help us.”
When he had seen the vision, we immediately sought to go on to Macedonia, concluding that God had called us to bring the good news to them.
verse.note: Here the narrative shifts without explanation from “they” to “we”, the first of several such passages in Acts. The traditional and still common view is that the author was a companion of Paul who joined the party at Troas. Others think he is drawing on a travel diary or using a literary convention.

verse.text: So, putting out to sea from Troas, we ran a straight course to Samothrace, and on the next day to Neapolis,
and from there to Philippi, which is a leading city of that district of Macedonia, a colony. We stayed in this city for some days.

note.term: a leading city of that district of Macedonia
note.traditional: the chief city of that part of Macedonia

verse.note: The manuscripts vary here, and the best-attested wording is awkward: literally “first city of the district of Macedonia”. Roman Macedonia was divided into four districts. Philippi lay in the first, but Amphipolis was that district’s capital and Thessalonica the provincial capital. Some editors therefore adopt a slightly different reading, “a city of the first district of Macedonia”; the rendering here follows the SBLGNT text and takes “first” as “leading”.

Luke uses the Latin word. A Roman colony was a city settled largely by army veterans, governed by Roman law with its own Roman-style magistrates, and its citizens held Roman citizenship. This explains the pride in being “Romans” in verse 21 and the officials named in the rest of the chapter.

verse.text: On the Sabbath day we went outside the gate to a riverside, where we supposed there was a place of prayer, and we sat down and spoke to the women who had gathered.
verse.note: The word ordinarily means “prayer”, but Jewish communities also used it for their meeting place, sometimes a building and sometimes an open-air spot near water. Whether Philippi had a synagogue building is unknown; that only women are mentioned may suggest a small community. Some manuscripts read instead “where prayer was customarily made”.

verse.text: A woman named Lydia was listening, a dealer in purple cloth from the city of Thyatira who worshiped God. The Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what Paul was saying.
verse.note: In Acts this expression describes Gentiles who were attached to the synagogue and worshiped Israel’s God without having become full converts to Judaism. Lydia is thus presented as a non-Jew who already revered the God of the Jews.

verse.text: When she and her household had been baptized, she appealed to us, saying, “If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come into my house and stay.” And she prevailed on us.
It happened that, as we were going to the place of prayer, a slave girl who had a spirit of divination met us; she brought her owners a great deal of profit by fortune-telling.
verse.note: The Greek is literally “a spirit, a python”. Python was the serpent of Delphi in Greek myth, slain by Apollo, whose oracle there was the most famous in the Greek world. By this period the word was used of soothsayers believed to have a spirit speaking through them. A first-century reader would have heard an association with pagan oracles that the English phrase does not carry.

verse.text: She followed Paul and us, crying out, “These men are slaves of the Most High God, who are proclaiming to you a way of salvation.”
verse.note: The Greek word is the ordinary term for a slave, a person owned by a master, and the speaker is herself a slave with owners. “Servants” is the traditional rendering and avoids the associations of modern slavery, but it suggests a hired employee, which the word did not mean.

The Greek has no article, so it may be “a way” or “the way” of salvation; most translations have “the way”. “Most High God” was used by Jews for the God of Israel, but pagans also used it for Zeus or another supreme deity. In a pagan city the girl’s cry could therefore be heard as announcing one path of deliverance from one high god among others, which may be part of why Paul silenced it.

verse.text: She kept doing this for many days. But Paul, exasperated, turned and said to the spirit, “I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her.” And it came out that very hour.
But when her owners saw that their hope of profit had gone out, they seized Paul and Silas and dragged them into the marketplace before the authorities,
and bringing them to the magistrates they said, “These men are throwing our city into turmoil. They are Jews,
verse.note: The Greek title was the usual equivalent of the Latin “praetor”. A Roman colony was headed by a pair of chief magistrates, and Luke gives them the Greek title commonly used for such officials. They had authority to hear charges and order punishment.

text.q: and they are proclaiming customs that it is not lawful for us, being Romans, to accept or practice.”

verse.text: The crowd joined in the attack against them, and the magistrates tore the clothes off them and ordered them to be beaten with rods.
After inflicting many blows on them, they threw them into prison, ordering the jailer to guard them securely.
Having received such an order, he threw them into the inner prison and fastened their feet in the stocks.
About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them.
Suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken; at once all the doors were opened, and everyone’s chains came loose.
The jailer woke up, and when he saw the doors of the prison open, he drew his sword and was about to kill himself, supposing that the prisoners had escaped.
But Paul called out in a loud voice, “Do yourself no harm, for we are all here!”
He called for lights and rushed in, and trembling he fell down before Paul and Silas.
Then he brought them outside and said, “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?”
verse.note: The jailer’s respectful address is the plural of the word translated “Lord” in the reply that follows, and “owners” in verses 16 and 19. The answer in verse 31 picks the word up and points him from these “lords” to the Lord Jesus.

verse.text: They said, “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household.”
And they spoke the word of the Lord to him, together with all who were in his house.
At that hour of the night he took them and washed their wounds, and at once he was baptized, he and all who belonged to him.
Then he brought them up into his house and set a meal before them, and he rejoiced with his whole household, having come to believe in God.
When day came, the magistrates sent the lictors, saying, “Release those men.”
verse.note: The Greek word, literally “rod-carrier”, was the standard term for Roman lictors, the attendants who walked before magistrates carrying bundles of rods and who carried out their orders, including beatings. It shares its root with “beaten with rods” in verse 22. “Police” suggests a modern institution that did not exist.

verse.text: The jailer reported these words to Paul: “The magistrates have sent word that you are to be released. So now come out and go in peace.”

But Paul said to them, “They beat us in public without trial, men who are Romans, and threw us into prison, and now they are throwing us out in secret? No indeed! Let them come themselves and lead us out.”
verse.note: “Romans” here means holders of Roman citizenship. Roman law protected citizens from being beaten or imprisoned without a proper trial, and officials who violated this could face serious consequences, hence the magistrates’ fear in verse 38. There is irony in the echo of verse 21, where the accusers had appealed to their own standing as Romans.

verse.text: The lictors reported these words to the magistrates, who were afraid when they heard that they were Romans.
So they came and appealed to them, and when they had led them out they asked them to leave the city.
After leaving the prison they went to Lydia’s house; and when they had seen the brothers and sisters, they encouraged them and departed.
After travelling through Amphipolis and Apollonia, they came to Thessalonica, where there was a synagogue of the Jews.
As was Paul’s custom, he went in to them, and on three Sabbaths he reasoned with them from the Scriptures,
explaining and setting out that the Messiah had to suffer and rise from the dead, and saying, “This is the Messiah: the Jesus I am proclaiming to you.”
verse.note: The Greek word is the one usually rendered 'Christ'. Here it is a title under discussion in a synagogue, the anointed king Israel expected, and 'Messiah' conveys what a Jewish hearer would have understood. Several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels and Acts.

verse.text: Some of them were persuaded and joined Paul and Silas, as did a great number of the Greek worshippers of God and not a few of the leading women.
verse.note: The term describes non-Jews who attached themselves to the synagogue and worshipped Israel's God without becoming full converts. 'Devout' suggests general piety, whereas Acts uses the word for this recognisable group (as again in verse 17). Many modern translations say 'God-fearing Greeks'.

verse.text: But the Jews became jealous. Taking with them some bad men from the marketplace rabble, they formed a mob and set the city in an uproar. They came to Jason’s house, seeking to bring them out before the assembly of the people.
When they did not find them, they dragged Jason and some brothers before the city magistrates, shouting, “These men who have thrown the world into turmoil have come here too,

note.traditional: rulers of the city; city authorities

verse.note: The Greek title is 'politarchs', the board of magistrates that governed Thessalonica and other Macedonian cities. The title is rare in ancient literature but is confirmed by inscriptions from Thessalonica itself.

text.q: and Jason has taken them in. They are all acting against Caesar’s decrees, saying that there is another king, Jesus.”

verse.text: They stirred up the crowd and the city magistrates, who heard all this,
and the magistrates took a bond from Jason and the others before releasing them.
verse.note: The Greek phrase mirrors a Latin legal expression for taking security. Jason and the others evidently gave a guarantee, probably money, that would be forfeited if there was further trouble. The exact terms are not stated.

verse.text: The brothers immediately sent Paul and Silas away by night to Beroea. When they arrived, they went to the synagogue of the Jews.
These were more noble-minded than those in Thessalonica: they received the word with all eagerness, examining the Scriptures every day to see whether these things were so.
So many of them believed, along with not a few Greek women of high standing, and men as well.
But when the Jews from Thessalonica learned that the word of God had been proclaimed by Paul in Beroea too, they came there as well, agitating and stirring up the crowds.
Then the brothers immediately sent Paul off to travel as far as the sea, but Silas and Timothy stayed behind there.
Those escorting Paul brought him as far as Athens, and they left with instructions for Silas and Timothy to come to him as quickly as possible.
While Paul was waiting for them in Athens, his spirit was provoked within him as he saw that the city was full of idols.
So he reasoned in the synagogue with the Jews and the worshippers of God, and in the marketplace every day with whoever happened to be there.

Some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers also debated with him. Some were saying, “What might this scrap-picker be trying to say?” Others said, “He seems to be a proclaimer of foreign divinities.” This was because he was announcing the good news of Jesus and the resurrection.
verse.note: The word was used of birds that pick up seed, and as slang for a person who scavenges scraps, whether of food in the market or of other people's ideas, and passes them on second-hand. 'Babbler' suggests only empty talk. The insult is that Paul is a dealer in borrowed ideas he does not understand.

In ordinary Greek this word meant a divine being or power, without the sense 'demon' it usually has elsewhere in the New Testament. The wording recalls the charge on which Socrates was tried in Athens, that of introducing new divinities. The plural may mean the hearers took 'Resurrection' (Anastasis) as the name of a goddess alongside Jesus; this suggestion goes back to ancient commentators but is not certain.

verse.text: They took hold of him and brought him to the Areopagus, saying, “May we know what this new teaching is that you are talking about?
verse.note: The Areopagus ('Hill of Ares') was both a rocky hill near the Acropolis and the name of the ancient Athenian council that had originally met there. The Greek can mean that Paul was taken to the hill or brought before the council, and scholars are divided on whether this was a formal hearing or an informal invitation to speak. 'In the middle of the Areopagus' (verse 22) and 'the Areopagite', meaning a member of the council (verse 34), fit the council somewhat better.

text.q: For you are bringing things that sound foreign to our ears, so we want to know what they mean.”

verse.text: Now all the Athenians and the foreigners living there had time for nothing but saying or hearing the newest thing.
Then Paul stood in the middle of the Areopagus and said, “Men of Athens, I see that in every way you are very religious.
verse.note: The Greek word could be praise ('devout') or criticism ('superstitious'), depending on the speaker's attitude. Most modern translations take it as a courteous opening, and that reading is followed here. Paul may have chosen a word that could be heard either way.

text.q: For as I walked around and looked carefully at your objects of worship, I even found an altar with the inscription, ‘To an unknown god.’ So what you worship without knowing it, this I proclaim to you.
The God who made the world and everything in it, being Lord of heaven and earth, does not live in temples made by hands,
nor is he served by human hands as if he needed anything, since he himself gives everyone life and breath and everything else.
From one he made every nation of humankind to live on the whole face of the earth, having marked out their appointed times and the boundaries of where they live,

verse.note: Many later manuscripts read 'from one blood', the reading behind the King James Version. The earliest witnesses have simply 'from one', which most scholars take to mean one man, Adam.

The Greek word for 'nation' is the same one rendered 'Gentiles' elsewhere, where it refers to the non-Jewish peoples. Here it means peoples in general. The phrase could also be read as 'the whole human race', taking it as a single collective, but most translations have 'every nation'.

text.q: so that they would seek God, if perhaps they might feel their way toward him and find him, though he is in fact not far from each one of us.
For in him we live and move and exist, as some of your own poets have also said: ‘For we too are his offspring.’

verse.note: The quoted line is from the Phaenomena of Aratus, a third-century BC poet from Cilicia, Paul's home region. A very similar line appears in the Stoic Cleanthes' Hymn to Zeus. In the poem 'his' refers to Zeus. The preceding words, 'in him we live and move and exist', are sometimes attributed to the Cretan poet Epimenides, but that attribution is disputed.

text.q: Since we are God’s offspring, then, we ought not to think that the divine is like gold or silver or stone, an image carved by human skill and imagination.
So God overlooked the times of ignorance, but now he commands all people everywhere to turn back,

verse.note: 'Repent' now suggests mainly feeling sorry. The Greek word carries the prophets' call to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct. Most translations keep 'repent' as an established term understood to include a change of life.

text.q: because he has set a day on which he is going to judge the world with justice by a man he has marked out, and he has given proof of this to everyone by raising him from the dead.”

verse.note: Greek has one word-family where English has two (righteous and just, righteousness and justice). This translation normally uses 'righteousness', but here the subject is fair judging, so 'justice' is the natural English. Most translations have 'in righteousness'; some have 'with justice'.

This is the word normally rendered 'faith' or 'faithfulness'. Here, with the verb 'provide', it has its other established sense of a pledge or proof given to win trust, so neither usual rendering fits. Nearly all translations have 'assurance' or 'proof'.

verse.text: When they heard of a resurrection of the dead, some began to scoff, but others said, “We will hear you on this again.”
So Paul went out from among them.
But some joined him and believed, among them Dionysius the Areopagite, a woman named Damaris, and others with them.
After this Paul left Athens and went to Corinth.
There he found a Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus, who had recently come from Italy with his wife Priscilla because Claudius had ordered all the Jews to leave Rome. He went to see them,

note.term: Claudius had ordered all the Jews to leave Rome

verse.note: The emperor Claudius (reigned AD 41–54) expelled Jews from Rome, an event the Roman biographer Suetonius also mentions. It is commonly dated to about AD 49, though the date is not certain. How thoroughly the order was enforced is also unknown; “all” may be a general statement.

verse.text: and because he was of the same trade he stayed with them and worked, for they were tentmakers by trade.
verse.note: The word is rare. It literally names a maker of tents, but many scholars think it covered leatherworking more broadly, since tents were often made of leather. The traditional rendering is kept because the narrower sense cannot be ruled out.

verse.text: Every sabbath he reasoned in the synagogue and tried to persuade both Jews and Greeks.
When Silas and Timothy came down from Macedonia, Paul gave himself wholly to the word, solemnly testifying to the Jews that the Messiah was Jesus.
verse.note: The Greek word is the one usually rendered “Christ”. Here it is a title under debate in a synagogue, the anointed king Israel expected, so “Messiah” is used, as several modern translations do. The Greek can also be read “that Jesus was the Messiah”; the sense is much the same.

verse.text: But when they opposed him and became abusive, he shook out his clothes and said to them, “Your blood be on your own head! I am clean of it. From now on I will go to the Gentiles.”
verse.note: Shaking out one's garments was a gesture of breaking off and disowning responsibility (compare Nehemiah 5:13). The words that follow echo the language of Ezekiel 33, where a watchman who has given warning is free of blame for the death of those who ignore it.

The Greek word means “peoples” or “nations”. In the plural, in Jewish usage, it refers to the non-Jewish peoples, and this translation then renders it “Gentiles”; elsewhere the same word appears as “nation” or “nations”.

verse.text: So he moved from there and went into the house of a man named Titius Justus, a worshipper of God, whose house was next door to the synagogue.
verse.note: In Acts this phrase describes Gentiles who attached themselves to the synagogue and honoured Israel's God without becoming full converts. Titius Justus bears a Roman name and was evidently such a person.

verse.text: Crispus, the synagogue leader, believed in the Lord together with his whole household, and many of the Corinthians who heard Paul believed and were baptized.
One night the Lord said to Paul in a vision, “Do not be afraid, but keep speaking and do not be silent,

text.q: for I am with you, and no one will attack you to harm you, because I have many people in this city.”

verse.text: So he settled there for a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them.
But while Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, the Jews rose up together against Paul and brought him before the tribunal,
verse.note: Gallio was the brother of the philosopher Seneca. An inscription found at Delphi places his term as governor of the province of Achaia in about AD 51–52, which makes this one of the firmest dates in the chronology of Paul's life. The tribunal was the raised platform from which a Roman magistrate heard cases.

verse.text: saying, “This man is persuading people to worship God contrary to the law.”
verse.note: The accusers do not say whether they mean Roman law or the Jewish law. They may have intended the charge to sound like a breach of Roman law; Gallio takes it as a dispute about “your own law” and dismisses it.

verse.text: Paul was about to open his mouth when Gallio said to the Jews, “If this were a matter of some wrongdoing or vicious crime, Jews, it would be reasonable for me to bear with you.

text.q: But if these are disputes about words and names and your own law, see to it yourselves. I have no wish to be a judge of these things.”

verse.text: And he drove them away from the tribunal.
Then they all seized Sosthenes, the synagogue leader, and began beating him in front of the tribunal. But none of this was of any concern to Gallio.
verse.note: The earliest manuscripts do not say who “all” are. Many later manuscripts add “the Greeks”, the reading behind the King James Version, making this a bystanders' attack on the Jewish leader; a few add “the Jews”. Either group is possible, and the text is left as open as the Greek.

verse.text: Paul stayed on for a good many days, then took leave of the brothers and sisters and sailed for Syria, and Priscilla and Aquila went with him. At Cenchreae he had his hair cut off, for he was under a vow.

note.term: he had his hair cut off

verse.note: Cenchreae was Corinth's eastern port, so the haircut preceded the sailing. In the Greek the one who cut his hair could be either Paul or Aquila, whose name stands immediately before; most interpreters take it to be Paul, the subject of the sentence. Cutting the hair normally marked the completion of a vow such as the Nazirite vow of Numbers 6, though Luke gives no details.

verse.text: They arrived in Ephesus, and there he left them. He himself went into the synagogue and reasoned with the Jews.
When they asked him to stay longer, he did not consent,
but took his leave and said, “I will come back to you again, if God wills.” He set sail from Ephesus,
landed at Caesarea, went up and greeted the assembly, and then went down to Antioch.
verse.note: The traditional rendering is “church”, which readers know but which now suggests a building or an institution. A first-century hearer knew the word as a civic gathering and as the Greek Old Testament's term for Israel assembled. This translation uses “assembly” throughout so that the reader can see it is one Greek word.

The Greek does not name the place. “Go up” and “go down” are the usual expressions for travelling to and from Jerusalem, so most interpreters understand a visit to the assembly in Jerusalem. A minority take it to mean going up from the harbour to the assembly in Caesarea.

verse.text: After spending some time there he set out and went from place to place through the Galatian region and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples.
Now a Jew named Apollos, a native of Alexandria, arrived in Ephesus. He was an eloquent man, powerful in the Scriptures.
He had been instructed in the way of the Lord, and being fervent in spirit he spoke and taught accurately the things about Jesus, though he knew only the baptism of John.
verse.note: The Greek is literally “boiling in the spirit”. It can describe Apollos's own ardent temperament, as rendered here, or mean that he was aglow with the Holy Spirit. The second reading is disputed because Apollos is said to have known only John's baptism.

verse.text: He began to speak boldly in the synagogue. When Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside and explained the way of God to him more accurately.
When he wanted to cross over to Achaia, the brothers and sisters encouraged him and wrote to the disciples to welcome him. On his arrival he was a great help to those who had believed through grace,
verse.note: The phrase stands at the end of the Greek sentence and can attach to either verb. The believers came to believe through grace, or Apollos through grace was a great help to them. The rendering follows the nearer connection.

verse.text: for he vigorously refuted the Jews in public, showing through the Scriptures that the Messiah was Jesus.
While Apollos was in Corinth, Paul traveled through the inland regions and came to Ephesus. There he found some disciples
and said to them, “Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?” They answered him, “No, we have not even heard that there is a Holy Spirit.”
He said, “Into what, then, were you baptized?” They said, “Into John’s baptism.”
Paul said, “John baptized with a baptism of turning back, telling the people to believe in the one coming after him, that is, in Jesus.”
verse.note: The traditional 'repentance' now suggests mainly feeling sorry. The Greek word, shaped by the prophets' call to 'return' to God, names a change of direction in mind and conduct. Most translations keep 'repentance' as an established term that readers understand to include a change of life.

verse.text: When they heard this, they were baptized into the name of the Lord Jesus.
