And when Paul laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came upon them, and they began to speak in tongues and prophesy.
There were about twelve men in all.
He went into the synagogue and for three months spoke boldly there, reasoning and persuading about the kingdom of God.

But when some became hardened and would not be persuaded, speaking ill of the Way in front of the congregation, he withdrew from them and took the disciples aside, reasoning daily in the lecture hall of Tyrannus.
verse.note: Most translations have 'refused to believe' or 'were disobedient', both of which the verb can mean. It is the negative counterpart of the verb 'persuading' in verse 8, and the rendering keeps that echo: Paul was persuading, and some would not be persuaded.

Acts uses 'the Way' as a name for the movement of Jesus's followers (for example 9:2 and again in verse 23 of this chapter). It was apparently an early self-designation, used before 'Christian' became common.

verse.text: This went on for two years, so that all who lived in Asia heard the word of the Lord, both Jews and Greeks.
God was doing no ordinary works of power through Paul’s hands,
so that even face-cloths or work aprons that had touched his skin were carried away to the sick, and their diseases left them and the evil spirits went out.
Then some of the itinerant Jewish exorcists also tried to invoke the name of the Lord Jesus over those who had evil spirits, saying, “I charge you by the Jesus whom Paul proclaims.”
Seven sons of a certain Sceva, a Jewish chief priest, were doing this.
verse.note: No Jewish high priest named Sceva is known from other sources. The word can also mean a member of one of the high-priestly families, and some scholars suspect the title was a claim made to impress clients. The matter is uncertain.

verse.text: But the evil spirit answered them, “Jesus I know, and Paul I know about; but you, who are you?”
Then the man in whom the evil spirit was leapt on them, subdued them all, and prevailed against them, so that they fled from that house naked and wounded.
verse.note: The Greek word normally means 'both', which would imply that only two of the seven sons were present. In later Koine it is also found meaning 'all' of more than two, and most translations take it that way here. Either reading is possible.

verse.text: This became known to all who lived in Ephesus, both Jews and Greeks. Fear fell on them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was held in high honor.
Many of those who had believed kept coming, confessing and disclosing their practices.
verse.note: The word can mean deeds in general, but it was also a technical term for magical procedures or spells. Given the next verse, the believers may be disclosing their spells specifically, which in magical thinking would rob them of their power. The rendering leaves both senses open.

verse.text: A good number of those who had practiced magic brought their books together and burned them in front of everyone. They added up their value and found it came to fifty thousand silver coins.
verse.note: The coin is not named but is probably the drachma, roughly a laborer's daily wage, so the sum is very large. The 'books' are scrolls of spells and formulas; Ephesus had a reputation for such writings.

verse.text: So mightily did the word of the Lord grow and prevail.
When these things had been completed, Paul resolved in the Spirit to pass through Macedonia and Achaia and go on to Jerusalem, saying, “After I have been there, I must also see Rome.”

note.traditional: purposed in the spirit / resolved in the Spirit

verse.note: The phrase may mean that Paul resolved under the guidance of the Holy Spirit, or simply that he resolved 'in his spirit', that is, made up his mind. Translations are divided. The following 'I must', which in Acts often signals divine necessity, slightly favors a reference to the Holy Spirit.

verse.text: He sent two of those who assisted him, Timothy and Erastus, to Macedonia, while he himself stayed on for a while in Asia.
About that time there arose no small disturbance concerning the Way.
For a man named Demetrius, a silversmith who made silver shrines of Artemis, brought the craftsmen no little business.
He gathered them together, along with the workers in related trades, and said, “Men, you know that our prosperity comes from this business,

text.q: and you see and hear that not only in Ephesus but in almost all of Asia this Paul has persuaded and turned away a considerable crowd, saying that gods made by hands are not gods.

The danger is not only that this line of work of ours will fall into disrepute, but also that the temple of the great goddess Artemis will be counted as nothing, and that she herself will be stripped of her majesty, she whom all Asia and the world worship.”

verse.text: When they heard this they were filled with rage and began shouting, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!”
The city was filled with confusion, and they rushed as one into the theater, dragging along Gaius and Aristarchus, Macedonians who were Paul’s traveling companions.
Paul wanted to go in among the people, but the disciples would not let him.
Even some of the chief officials of Asia, who were friends of his, sent word to him urging him not to venture into the theater.
verse.note: The Greek title is 'Asiarchs'. These were wealthy leading citizens who held a high office or honorific rank in the province of Asia. Their exact duties are debated; many scholars connect them with the provincial council and its public festivals. That such men were friendly to Paul is notable.

verse.text: Some were shouting one thing, some another, for the assembly was in confusion, and most of them did not know why they had come together.
verse.note: The Greek word here is the ordinary term for a gathering of a city's citizens. The same word names the community of believers elsewhere in the New Testament, where it is traditionally translated 'church'. This translation uses 'assembly' in both settings so the reader can see it is one word. The 'lawful assembly' of verse 39 is the regular, legally convened citizens' meeting, in contrast to this irregular one.

verse.text: Some of the crowd instructed Alexander, whom the Jews had pushed forward, and Alexander motioned with his hand, wanting to make a defense to the people.

note.traditional: they drew Alexander out of the multitude / prompted Alexander

verse.note: The sentence is obscure. The verb can mean 'instruct' or 'advise', giving the sense that people in the crowd briefed or prompted Alexander. It can also mean 'conclude', so that some of the crowd concluded Alexander was responsible. Some manuscripts have a different verb meaning 'pushed forward'. Why the Jews put him forward is not stated; perhaps to dissociate their community from Paul.

verse.text: But when they recognized that he was a Jew, a single cry went up from them all, and for about two hours they shouted, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!”

When the city clerk had calmed the crowd, he said, “Men of Ephesus, what person is there who does not know that the city of the Ephesians is temple-guardian of the great Artemis and of the image that fell from the sky?

note.term: temple-guardian of the great Artemis and of the image that fell from the sky
note.traditional: temple keeper of the great Artemis and of the sacred stone that fell from the sky

verse.note: 'Temple-guardian' was a title of honor that cities claimed, and it is attested for Ephesus in inscriptions. The Greek for the second item is a single word meaning 'fallen from Zeus' or 'fallen from the sky', with no noun attached. It probably refers to a sacred object, perhaps a meteorite or an ancient image, believed to be of heavenly origin; the clerk's point is that it was not 'made by hands'.

text.q: Since these things are undeniable, you ought to stay calm and do nothing rash.
For you have brought these men here, who are neither temple robbers nor blasphemers of our goddess.
So if Demetrius and the craftsmen with him have a complaint against anyone, the courts are in session and there are proconsuls; let them bring charges against one another.
But if you are seeking anything beyond that, it will be settled in the lawful assembly.

verse.text: For we are in danger of being charged with rioting over today’s events, since there is no cause for it, and we will not be able to give an account of this commotion.” Having said this, he dismissed the assembly.
After the uproar had died down, Paul sent for the disciples and encouraged them; then he said farewell and set out to go to Macedonia.
After travelling through those parts and encouraging the people there with many words, he came to Greece
and spent three months there. When a plot was made against him by the Jews as he was about to sail for Syria, he decided to return through Macedonia.
He was accompanied by Sopater son of Pyrrhus, from Beroea; by Aristarchus and Secundus, from Thessalonica; by Gaius from Derbe, and Timothy; and by Tychicus and Trophimus, from Asia.
verse.note: Asia here and throughout the chapter is the Roman province of that name, the western part of modern Turkey, with Ephesus as its chief city. It is not the continent.

verse.text: These men came and were waiting for us at Troas;
verse.note: The manuscripts are divided between two verbs that differ by a single letter: 'having come' and 'having gone ahead'. The Greek text translated here prints the first; many editions and most English versions follow the second. The sense of the passage is little affected.

The narrative switches here to the first person plural, which it last used at Philippi in chapter 16. The usual explanation is that the author, or a source he draws on, rejoined Paul's party at Philippi. The nature of these 'we' passages remains debated.

verse.text: but we sailed from Philippi after the days of Unleavened Bread and within five days came to them at Troas, where we stayed seven days.
On the first day of the week, when we had gathered to break bread, Paul was addressing them. Since he was going to leave the next day, he kept on speaking until midnight.

note.term: On the first day of the week

verse.note: The Greek idiom is literally 'the first of the sabbaths', the day after the Sabbath. It is disputed whether Luke counts days from sunset, in the Jewish manner, which would make this Saturday night, or from dawn, which would make it Sunday night. This is one of the earliest references to believers gathering on this day.

verse.text: There were many lamps in the upstairs room where we were gathered.

A young man named Eutychus was sitting on the windowsill, sinking into a deep sleep as Paul went on speaking at length. Overcome by sleep, he fell from the third story to the ground below and was picked up dead.
But Paul went down, threw himself on him, and putting his arms around him said, “Do not be alarmed, for his life is in him.”
Then he went back up, broke the bread and ate, and after talking with them a long while, until dawn, he left.
They took the boy away alive, and were comforted more than a little.
As for us, we went ahead to the ship and set sail for Assos, intending to take Paul on board there; for that is what he had arranged, since he himself intended to travel by land.
When he met us at Assos, we took him on board and came to Mitylene.
Sailing from there, we arrived the next day off Chios; the day after, we crossed over to Samos; and the day after that, we came to Miletus.
For Paul had decided to sail past Ephesus, so that he would not have to spend time in Asia; he was hurrying to be in Jerusalem, if it were possible for him, on the day of Pentecost.
From Miletus he sent to Ephesus and summoned the elders of the assembly.
verse.note: The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering, used that way in the preceding chapter, and the Septuagint's term for Israel assembled. 'Church' is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. 'Assembly' is used throughout this translation so that the one Greek word is visible as one word.

verse.text: When they came to him, he said to them, “You yourselves know how, from the first day I set foot in Asia, I was with you the whole time,

text.q: serving the Lord as a slave with all humility, with tears, and with the trials that came upon me through the plots of the Jews;

note.term: serving the Lord as a slave

verse.note: The verb is the one used for the service a slave owes a master, not a general word for serving. Most translations have simply 'serving', which loses the image of belonging wholly to the Lord. Some scholars note that 'slave of the Lord' also echoes an honorific Septuagint title for Moses and the prophets.

text.q: how I did not hold back from declaring to you anything that would benefit you, and from teaching you in public and from house to house,
testifying solemnly to both Jews and Greeks about turning back to God and faith in our Lord Jesus.

verse.note: Most translations keep 'repentance' as an established term understood to include a change of life. In modern English, however, the word centres on feeling sorry, whereas the Greek carries the prophets' call to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct.

text.q: And now, look, bound by the Spirit, I am going to Jerusalem, not knowing what will happen to me there,

verse.note: The Greek can mean that Paul is bound by the Holy Spirit, or that he is bound in his own spirit, that is, inwardly compelled. The mention of the Holy Spirit in the next verse favours the first, which most recent translations follow. 'Bound' anticipates the literal chains of the next verse.

text.q: except that the Holy Spirit testifies solemnly to me in city after city, saying that chains and afflictions await me.
But I do not count my life worth anything or precious to myself, so long as I complete my course and the service I received from the Lord Jesus: to testify solemnly to the good news of God’s grace.
And now, look, I know that all of you, among whom I went about proclaiming the kingdom, will not see my face again.
Therefore I testify to you this very day that I am clean of the blood of all,

note.term: clean of the blood of all
note.traditional: innocent of the blood of all

verse.note: The image is that of the watchman in Ezekiel 3 and 33: if he fails to sound the warning, the blood of those who die is on his hands. Paul claims to have discharged that responsibility, as he did with similar words at Corinth in Acts 18:6.

text.q: for I did not hold back from declaring to you the whole purpose of God.
Keep watch over yourselves and over the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has placed you as overseers, to shepherd the assembly of God, which he acquired through the blood of his Own.

verse.note: This is the word that later became 'bishop'. Here it is applied to the same people called 'elders' in verse 17, so the two terms describe one group of local leaders. It is not yet a distinct office above the elders.

The Greek can be read 'his own blood' or 'the blood of his own one', meaning his Son; 'his own' was a term of endearment for close kin. The traditional rendering takes it the first way, and many scholars and several recent translations take it the second. There is also a manuscript variant: some read 'the assembly of the Lord' instead of 'of God', which may have arisen to ease the difficulty of speaking of God's blood.

text.q: I know that after my departure savage wolves will come in among you, not sparing the flock,
and from among your own selves men will arise speaking twisted things, to draw the disciples away after them.
Therefore stay awake, remembering that for three years, night and day, I did not stop warning each one of you with tears.
And now I entrust you to God and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up and to give you the inheritance among all those who have been made holy.
I coveted no one’s silver or gold or clothing.
You yourselves know that these hands served my own needs and those of the people with me.
In everything I showed you that by working hard in this way we must help the weak, and remember the words of the Lord Jesus, that he himself said, ‘It is more blessed to give than to receive.’”

note.term: It is more blessed to give than to receive

verse.note: This saying of Jesus is not recorded in any of the four Gospels. It is one of the few sayings attributed to him elsewhere in the New Testament, and shows that his words also circulated independently of the written Gospels.

verse.text: When he had said these things, he knelt down with them all and prayed.
There was much weeping from them all; they threw their arms around Paul’s neck and kissed him again and again,
grieving most of all over the word he had spoken, that they were not going to see his face again. Then they escorted him to the ship.
When we had torn ourselves away from them and set sail, we ran a straight course and came to Cos, the next day to Rhodes, and from there to Patara.
Finding a ship crossing over to Phoenicia, we went aboard and set sail.
We came in sight of Cyprus and, leaving it on our left, sailed on to Syria and landed at Tyre, for there the ship was to unload its cargo.
We sought out the disciples and stayed there seven days. Through the Spirit they kept telling Paul not to go on to Jerusalem.
When our days there were up, we left and went on our way, and all of them, with wives and children, escorted us until we were outside the city. Kneeling on the beach, we prayed
and said farewell to one another. Then we boarded the ship, and they returned home.
We completed the voyage from Tyre and arrived at Ptolemais, and after greeting the brothers and sisters we stayed with them one day.
verse.note: The Greek plural was the ordinary way to address or describe a mixed group of men and women, and here it refers to the whole local community of believers. ‘Brothers’ alone now suggests men only. Many recent translations make the same choice; others keep ‘brothers’ as the more literal form.

verse.text: The next day we left and came to Caesarea, and we went into the house of Philip the evangelist, who was one of the Seven, and stayed with him.
verse.note: The Seven are the men appointed in Jerusalem to oversee the daily distribution of food (Acts 6:1–6). The description distinguishes this Philip, who had preached in Samaria and to the Ethiopian official (Acts 8), from Philip the apostle.

verse.text: He had four unmarried daughters who prophesied.
verse.note: The word denotes a young woman who has not married, with virginity assumed and not separately asserted. The point here is the daughters’ status in their father’s household, so ‘unmarried’ conveys what a first-century reader would have taken from it. Some interpreters think a deliberate commitment to celibacy is implied, but the text does not say so.

verse.text: While we were staying there for a number of days, a prophet named Agabus came down from Judea.

He came to us, took Paul’s belt, bound his own feet and hands, and said, “This is what the Holy Spirit says: ‘In this way the Jews in Jerusalem will bind the man who owns this belt and hand him over into the hands of Gentiles.’”
verse.note: One Greek word means both ‘a nation’ or ‘people’ and, in the plural, the non-Jewish peoples as a group. This translation uses ‘Gentiles’ for the second sense and ‘nation’ or ‘nations’ for the first; both render the same word.

verse.text: When we heard this, we and the local people begged him not to go up to Jerusalem.
Then Paul answered, “What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart? For I am ready not only to be bound but even to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus.”
Since he would not be persuaded, we fell silent, saying, “The Lord’s will be done.”
After these days we got ready and started up to Jerusalem.
Some of the disciples from Caesarea also came with us, bringing us to the man with whom we were to lodge, Mnason, a Cypriot and a disciple from the early days.

note.term: bringing us to the man with whom we were to lodge

verse.note: The Greek is compressed and can also be read as ‘bringing with them Mnason, with whom we were to lodge’. Most translations take it as rendered here. It is also unclear whether Mnason’s house was in Jerusalem or at a stopping place on the two-day journey from Caesarea.

verse.text: When we arrived in Jerusalem, the brothers and sisters welcomed us gladly.
The next day Paul went in with us to James, and all the elders were present.
After greeting them, he recounted one by one the things God had done among the Gentiles through his service.
verse.note: The word means service rendered or a task carried out on someone’s behalf. ‘Ministry’ is the traditional rendering and is still used by most translations, but it now suggests a clerical profession or office, which the Greek word does not.

verse.text: When they heard it, they glorified God, and they said to him, “You see, brother, how many tens of thousands there are among the Jews who have believed, and all of them are zealous for the law.

text.q: They have been told about you that you teach all the Jews living among the Gentiles to turn away from Moses, telling them not to circumcise their children or live by the customs.
What then is to be done? They will certainly hear that you have come.

note.term: They will certainly hear that you have come.
note.traditional: the multitude must needs come together: for they will hear that thou art come

verse.note: Many later manuscripts have a longer reading: ‘a crowd must certainly gather, for they will hear that you have come.’ The shorter text translated here is found in several early witnesses and is the one printed in the SBLGNT.

text.q: So do what we tell you. We have four men who have taken a vow on themselves.

Take them, be purified with them, and pay their expenses so that they may shave their heads. Then everyone will know that there is nothing in what they have been told about you, but that you yourself also keep in step, observing the law.

verse.note: The vow is generally understood to be a Nazirite vow (Numbers 6), which ended with shaving the head and offering several sacrifices at the temple. Paying for the offerings of Nazirites who could not afford them was regarded as an act of piety. How Paul’s own purification relates to the men’s vow is debated.

text.q: As for the Gentiles who have believed, we have sent word of our decision that they should keep away from what has been sacrificed to idols, from blood, from what has been strangled, and from sexual immorality.”

verse.text: Then Paul took the men, and the next day, having been purified with them, he went into the temple, giving notice of the completion of the days of purification, when the offering would be made for each one of them.
When the seven days were almost over, the Jews from Asia, seeing him in the temple, threw the whole crowd into confusion and laid hands on him,

shouting, “Men of Israel, help! This is the man who teaches everyone everywhere against the people and the law and this place. What is more, he has even brought Greeks into the temple and has defiled this holy place.”
verse.note: Non-Jews were allowed in the outer court of the temple, but a barrier marked off the inner courts, with notices warning that any foreigner who passed it would be liable to death. Josephus describes these notices, and inscribed examples have been found. The charge was therefore a capital one.

verse.text: For they had earlier seen Trophimus the Ephesian in the city with him, and they supposed that Paul had brought him into the temple.
The whole city was roused, and the people came running together. They took hold of Paul and dragged him out of the temple, and at once the doors were shut.
While they were trying to kill him, a report went up to the tribune of the cohort that all Jerusalem was in confusion.
verse.note: The Greek title, literally ‘commander of a thousand’, was the standard equivalent for a Roman military tribune. He commanded the cohort garrisoned in the Antonia fortress, which overlooked the temple courts and was connected to them by stairs. That is why the report ‘went up’ and the soldiers ‘ran down’. He is named in Acts 23:26 as Claudius Lysias.

verse.text: At once he took soldiers and centurions and ran down to them. When they saw the tribune and the soldiers, they stopped beating Paul.
Then the tribune came up, took hold of him, and ordered him to be bound with two chains; and he began asking who he was and what he had done.
Some in the crowd were shouting one thing, some another. Since he could not learn the facts because of the uproar, he ordered him to be taken into the barracks.
When Paul reached the steps, he had to be carried by the soldiers because of the violence of the crowd,
for the mass of the people was following, shouting, “Away with him!”
As he was about to be brought into the barracks, Paul said to the tribune, “May I say something to you?” He said, “You know Greek?

text.q: Then you are not the Egyptian who some time ago stirred up a revolt and led the four thousand men of the Assassins out into the wilderness?”

verse.note: The Greek borrows a Latin word for a man armed with a dagger, which was used for a murderer or assassin. Josephus applies it to Jewish militants of this period who stabbed their opponents in crowds. He also tells of an Egyptian prophet who led a large following to the Mount of Olives under the governor Felix and escaped when the Romans attacked. His figures for the Egyptian’s following differ from the number given here.

verse.text: Paul said, “I am a Jew, from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no insignificant city. I beg you, allow me to speak to the people.”
When he had given permission, Paul stood on the steps and motioned with his hand to the people. When a great silence had fallen, he addressed them in the Hebrew language, saying:

note.traditional: in the Hebrew tongue; in Aramaic

verse.note: The Greek says literally ‘in the Hebrew dialect’. Many scholars take this to mean Aramaic, the everyday language of many Jews in Judea, since Greek writers could call either language ‘Hebrew’. Others argue that Hebrew proper is meant. The question is unresolved, and the text is rendered literally.

text.q: “Brothers and fathers, listen to the defense I now make before you.”

verse.text: When they heard that he was addressing them in the Hebrew language, they became even quieter. And he said:

note.traditional: the Hebrew tongue / the Hebrew dialect

verse.note: The Greek phrase means the language of the Hebrews. Most scholars think this was Aramaic, the everyday language of Jewish Palestine, and some translations say 'Aramaic' outright. Others argue that Hebrew itself is meant. The literal wording is kept because the Greek does not settle the question.

text.q: “I am a Jew, born in Tarsus of Cilicia but brought up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel, trained according to the strictness of our ancestral law, and zealous for God, just as all of you are today.

note.term: brought up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel
note.traditional: brought up in this city, educated at the feet of Gamaliel

verse.note: The Greek can be punctuated two ways. 'At the feet of Gamaliel' may go with 'brought up in this city', as here and in the SBLGNT punctuation, or with 'trained' ('educated at the feet of Gamaliel according to the strictness of our ancestral law'), as in many English versions. Either way Paul claims a Jerusalem upbringing and schooling under Gamaliel, a leading Pharisaic teacher.

text.q: I persecuted this Way to the death, binding both men and women and handing them over to prisons,

verse.note: 'The Way' (literally 'the road') is the name Acts uses for the movement of Jesus's followers, apparently their own term for themselves. Paul uses it here without explanation, assuming the crowd knows which group he means.

text.q: as the high priest and the whole council of elders can testify for me. From them I also received letters to the brothers in Damascus, and I was on my way there to bring those who were there as well to Jerusalem in chains to be punished.
Now as I was on my way and getting near Damascus, about midday a great light from heaven suddenly flashed around me,
and I fell to the ground and heard a voice saying to me,
‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?’
I answered, ‘Who are you, Lord?’ And he said to me,
‘I am Jesus the Nazarene, whom you are persecuting.’

verse.note: The Greek does not name the town but uses a descriptive title, Nazōraios, attached to Jesus. Most translations render it 'of Nazareth', which is how it was generally understood. The form is kept as a title here because Acts later uses the same word in the plural for Jesus's followers (24:5).

text.q: Those who were with me saw the light but did not hear the voice of the one who was speaking to me.

verse.note: Acts 9:7 says Paul's companions heard the voice, which seems to conflict with this verse. Some translations resolve the tension by rendering 'did not understand the voice' here, appealing to a difference in the grammatical case used with 'hear'. That distinction is disputed and not reliably observed in Greek of the period, so the plain rendering is kept.

text.q: I said, ‘What should I do, Lord?’ And the Lord said to me,
‘Get up and go into Damascus, and there you will be told about everything that has been appointed for you to do.’
Since I could not see because of the glory of that light, those who were with me led me by the hand, and so I came into Damascus.
A certain Ananias, a man devout by the standard of the law and well spoken of by all the Jews living there,
came to me, stood beside me, and said, ‘Brother Saul, see again!’ And at that very moment I could see again, and I looked up at him.
Then he said, ‘The God of our ancestors has appointed you to know his will, to see the Righteous One, and to hear a voice from his own mouth,

note.traditional: the Just One / the Righteous One

verse.note: This is a title for the Messiah, used also in Acts 3:14 and 7:52. Greek has a single word-family where English has two (righteous/just, righteousness/justice), so 'the Just One' translates the same word. Older versions use that form.

text.q: because you will be his witness to all people of what you have seen and heard.
And now, why are you waiting? Get up, be baptized, and wash away your sins, calling on his name.’
After I had returned to Jerusalem, while I was praying in the temple, I fell into a trance
and saw him saying to me,
‘Hurry, get out of Jerusalem quickly, because they will not accept your testimony about me.’
And I said, ‘Lord, they themselves know that I went from synagogue to synagogue imprisoning and beating those who believed in you.
And when the blood of Stephen your witness was being shed, I myself was standing by, approving, and guarding the cloaks of those who were killing him.’

verse.note: The Greek word is the ordinary one for a witness, the same word used of Paul himself in verse 15. The English 'martyr' derives from it, but the sense 'one who dies for the faith' developed later, partly from cases like Stephen's. Most modern translations render 'witness' here.

text.q: And he said to me,
‘Go, for I will send you far away to the Gentiles.’”

verse.note: The same Greek word means 'nations' or 'peoples', and in the plural commonly refers to the non-Jewish peoples. English translations divide it between 'nations' and 'Gentiles' according to context. The crowd erupts at this word because of the claim that God was sending Paul away from Jerusalem to non-Jews.

verse.text: They had been listening to him up to this statement, but then they raised their voices, saying, “Rid the earth of such a man! He should not be allowed to live!”
As they were shouting, throwing off their cloaks, and flinging dust into the air,
the commander ordered him to be brought into the barracks, saying that he should be examined by flogging, so that he could find out the reason they were shouting against him like this.
verse.note: The Greek title, literally 'commander of a thousand', was the standard equivalent of the Roman military tribune. This officer commanded the cohort garrisoned in the fortress beside the temple and is named in 23:26 as Claudius Lysias. English versions vary between 'tribune' and 'commander'.

verse.text: But when they had stretched him out with the straps, Paul said to the centurion standing by, “Is it lawful for you to flog a man who is a Roman citizen and has not been condemned?”

note.traditional: bound him with thongs / stretched him out for the whips

verse.note: The Greek word normally means a leather strap or thong. The phrase can mean that Paul was stretched out and tied with straps, as rendered here, or stretched out 'for the lashes', that is, for the whip. Translations are divided, and either way he is being positioned for the flogging ordered in verse 24.

'Roman' here means a holder of Roman citizenship, not a native of Rome. Roman law protected citizens from being bound or flogged without trial, and an officer who violated this could face serious consequences, which explains the commander's fear in verse 29. Citizenship could be inherited, granted, or, as the commander says of himself, obtained at considerable cost.

verse.text: When the centurion heard this, he went to the commander and reported it, saying, “What are you about to do? This man is a Roman citizen.”
The commander came and said to him, “Tell me, are you a Roman citizen?” He said, “Yes.”
The commander answered, “I acquired this citizenship for a large sum of money.” Paul said, “But I was born a citizen.”
So those who were about to examine him drew back from him at once, and the commander himself was afraid when he realized that Paul was a Roman citizen and that he had put him in chains.

The next day, wanting to know for certain what he was being accused of by the Jews, he released him and ordered the chief priests and the whole council to assemble. Then he brought Paul down and stood him before them.
Paul looked intently at the council and said, “Brothers, I have lived my life before God in all good conscience to this day.”
But the high priest Ananias ordered those standing beside him to strike him on the mouth.
verse.note: This is Ananias son of Nedebaeus, high priest from about AD 47 to the late 50s, not the Annas of the Gospels. Josephus portrays him as wealthy and grasping, and he was killed by Jewish insurgents at the outbreak of the revolt against Rome in AD 66.

verse.text: Then Paul said to him, “God is going to strike you, you whitewashed wall! You sit there judging me according to the law, and yet in violation of the law you order me to be struck?”
verse.note: The image is of a clean coat of plaster hiding something unsound or unclean beneath it. It echoes Ezekiel 13:10-15, where a flimsy wall daubed with whitewash is destined to fall, and resembles Jesus's ‘whitewashed tombs’ in Matthew 23:27. Paul's charge is that a judge who orders a blow before any verdict is himself breaking the law he claims to apply.

verse.text: Those standing by said, “Are you insulting God’s high priest?”
And Paul said, “I did not know, brothers, that he was high priest; for it is written, ‘You shall not speak evil of a ruler of your people.’”
verse.note: It is disputed whether Paul truly failed to recognise the high priest (the hearing was irregular and convened by a Roman officer) or is speaking with irony, implying that no one behaving this way could be taken for a high priest. The Greek allows either, and the translation leaves the question open. The quotation is from Exodus 22:28.

verse.text: Now when Paul realized that one part were Sadducees and the other Pharisees, he cried out in the council, “Brothers, I am a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees. I am on trial concerning the hope and the resurrection of the dead.”
When he said this, a dispute broke out between the Pharisees and the Sadducees, and the assembly was split.
For Sadducees say there is no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit, while Pharisees affirm them all.
verse.note: The Greek word normally means ‘both’, though three things have just been listed. In the Greek of this period it can be used loosely for more than two, which is the reading taken here. Others keep ‘both’ and understand two items: resurrection on the one hand, and angel-or-spirit on the other.

verse.text: A great outcry arose, and some of the scribes from the Pharisees’ party stood up and contended fiercely, saying, “We find nothing wrong in this man. And if a spirit has spoken to him, or an angel—”

note.traditional: let us not fight against God

verse.note: In the earliest manuscripts the sentence breaks off unfinished, as if drowned out by the uproar. Many later manuscripts complete it with ‘let us not fight against God’, probably borrowed from Acts 5:39, and the King James Version follows them. The text here follows the shorter reading.

verse.text: As the dispute grew violent, the commander, afraid that Paul would be torn apart by them, ordered the troops to go down, snatch him from their midst, and bring him into the barracks.
verse.note: The Greek title, literally ‘leader of a thousand’, was the standard equivalent for a Roman military tribune, here the officer commanding the cohort stationed in Jerusalem. His name, Claudius Lysias, appears in verse 26. The ‘barracks’ are generally identified with the Antonia fortress overlooking the temple courts, which is why the troops ‘go down’.

verse.text: The following night the Lord stood by him and said, “Take courage! For as you have testified fully about me in Jerusalem, so you must also testify in Rome.”
When day came, the Jews banded together and bound themselves under a curse, declaring that they would neither eat nor drink until they had killed Paul.

note.traditional: bound themselves under a curse; bound themselves by an oath

verse.note: The verb means to call down a curse on oneself if a vow is not kept; in effect, ‘may God destroy us if we fail’. It is stronger than an ordinary oath, and verse 14 intensifies it further with a doubled expression.

verse.text: There were more than forty who formed this conspiracy.
They went to the chief priests and the elders and said, “We have bound ourselves under a solemn curse to taste nothing until we have killed Paul.

text.q: So now you, together with the council, notify the commander to bring him down to you, as though you were going to examine his case more closely. And we are ready to kill him before he gets near.”

verse.text: But the son of Paul’s sister heard of the ambush, and he came, entered the barracks, and reported it to Paul.
Paul called one of the centurions and said, “Take this young man to the commander, for he has something to report to him.”
So he took him, brought him to the commander, and said, “The prisoner Paul called me and asked me to bring this young man to you, as he has something to tell you.”
The commander took him by the hand, drew him aside, and asked privately, “What is it that you have to report to me?”
He said, “The Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul down to the council tomorrow, as though it were going to inquire somewhat more closely about him.

note.term: as though it were going to inquire

verse.note: Manuscripts differ over who is said to be about to inquire: the council (‘it’), the Jews (‘they’), or the commander (‘you’). The text translated here makes the council the subject. The pretext is the same in each case.

text.q: So do not be persuaded by them, for more than forty of their men are lying in ambush for him. They have bound themselves under a curse neither to eat nor to drink until they have killed him, and now they are ready, waiting for your consent.”

verse.text: So the commander dismissed the young man, ordering him, “Tell no one that you have notified me of this.”
Then he called two of the centurions and said, “Get two hundred soldiers ready to go as far as Caesarea, with seventy horsemen and two hundred spearmen, to leave at the third hour of the night.
verse.note: The meaning of this word is uncertain. It occurs nowhere else in surviving Greek until centuries later, and its form suggests something held in or taken by the right hand. ‘Spearmen’ is the traditional guess, and other proposals include light-armed troops or slingers; the translation keeps the traditional rendering for want of better evidence.

note.term: the third hour of the night

verse.note: Night hours were counted from sunset, so this is roughly nine in the evening. The size of the escort, about half the Jerusalem garrison, shows how seriously the commander took the threat to a Roman citizen in his custody.

text.q: Provide mounts as well, so that they can put Paul on them and bring him safely to Felix the governor.”

verse.text: And he wrote a letter to this effect:

text.q: “Claudius Lysias, to His Excellency the governor Felix: greetings.
This man was seized by the Jews and was about to be killed by them when I came upon them with the troops and rescued him, having learned that he is a Roman citizen.

note.term: having learned that he is a Roman citizen
note.traditional: having understood that he was a Roman

verse.note: ‘Roman’ here means a holder of Roman citizenship, not a native of Rome. In Luke's narrative (21:31-33; 22:24-29) the commander discovered Paul's citizenship only after arresting him and ordering him flogged. The letter rearranges events to put its writer in a better light, and Luke lets the reader notice this.

text.q: Wanting to know the charge on which they were accusing him, I brought him down to their council.
I found that he was being accused over disputed points of their law, but that there was no charge against him deserving death or imprisonment.
When it was disclosed to me that there would be a plot against the man, I sent him to you at once, and I have also ordered his accusers to state their case against him before you.”

verse.text: So the soldiers, in accordance with their orders, took Paul and brought him by night to Antipatris.
The next day they let the horsemen go on with him and returned to the barracks.
When the horsemen entered Caesarea and delivered the letter to the governor, they also presented Paul to him.
After reading it, he asked what province he was from, and on learning that he was from Cilicia,
“I will give you a full hearing,” he said, “when your accusers also arrive.” And he ordered that he be kept under guard in Herod’s palace.
verse.note: The Greek borrows the Latin praetorium, the official residence and headquarters of a Roman governor. In Caesarea this was the palace built by Herod the Great, taken over by the Roman administration. ‘Palace’ is used because the building is identified by its builder; some translations keep ‘praetorium’ or use ‘headquarters’.

verse.text: Five days later the high priest Ananias came down with some elders and an advocate, a certain Tertullus, and they presented their case against Paul to the governor.
verse.note: The Greek word means a trained public speaker, and older English versions have 'orator'. In a courtroom setting it meant a professional pleader hired to present a case, so 'advocate' is used here. Most modern translations similarly have 'lawyer' or 'attorney'.

verse.text: When Paul had been called in, Tertullus began to accuse him, saying: “Since through you we enjoy much peace, and since reforms are being carried out for this nation through your foresight,
verse.note: The same Greek word is translated 'nation' when it means a people as a unit, as here of the Jewish people (also verses 10 and 17), and 'Gentiles' when its plural means the non-Jewish peoples. English needs two words where Greek has one.

text.q: in every way and in every place we welcome this, most excellent Felix, with all gratitude.
But so as not to detain you any longer, I beg you, in your forbearance, to hear us briefly.
For we have found this man to be a plague, one who stirs up riots among all the Jews throughout the world, and a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes.

verse.note: The word meant a school of thought or party, and Acts uses it neutrally of the Pharisees and Sadducees. It did not yet carry the later sense of 'heresy', though Tertullus plainly means it dismissively and Paul in verse 14 declines the label. The same English word is used in both verses so the echo can be heard.

text.q: He even tried to desecrate the temple, and so we seized him.

note.traditional: includes verse 7: 'and would have judged him according to our law. But the commander Lysias came and with great violence took him out of our hands, commanding his accusers to come to you'

verse.note: Some later manuscripts add a longer passage here, numbered as the end of verse 6, verse 7 and the start of verse 8. It is absent from the earliest witnesses and is omitted in the Greek text translated here, which is why the numbering passes from 6 to 8. Without it, 'him' in verse 8 is Paul; with it, the person Felix is to examine would be Lysias.

text.q: If you examine him yourself, you will be able to find out from him about all these things of which we accuse him.”

verse.text: The Jews also joined in the attack, asserting that these things were so.
When the governor nodded to him to speak, Paul replied: “Knowing that for many years you have been a judge for this nation, I make my defense with good cheer.

text.q: As you can verify, it is no more than twelve days since I went up to Jerusalem to worship,
and they did not find me arguing with anyone or stirring up a crowd, either in the temple or in the synagogues or anywhere in the city.
Nor can they prove to you the things of which they now accuse me.

But this I do admit to you: it is according to the Way, which they call a sect, that I serve the God of our ancestors, believing everything that accords with the Law and everything written in the Prophets,

verse.note: The ordinary word for a road or path is used in Acts as a name the followers of Jesus gave their own movement. Paul sets this name against his accusers' label 'sect'.

Most English versions have 'worship' here. The verb refers to religious service rendered to a deity, and it differs from the word translated 'worship' in verse 11, which refers to an act of homage. 'Serve' keeps the two distinct; some translations do the same.

text.q: and having a hope in God, a hope that these men themselves also hold, that there is going to be a resurrection of both the righteous and the unrighteous.
For this reason I too always strive to keep my conscience clear before God and before people.
After several years away, I came to bring gifts for the poor to my nation, and offerings.
I was engaged in these when they found me in the temple, purified, with no crowd and no uproar.
But some Jews from Asia—they ought to be here before you and bring their charges, if they have anything against me.

note.term: But some Jews from Asia—they ought to be here

verse.note: Paul's sentence breaks off in the Greek without a main verb, and the translation keeps the break. 'Asia' is the Roman province in the west of modern Turkey, with Ephesus as its chief city, not the continent. These were the people who started the uproar in the temple (Acts 21:27), and Paul's point is that the actual witnesses are absent.

text.q: Or let these men themselves say what wrongdoing they found when I stood before the council,
unless it is this one thing that I cried out as I stood among them: ‘It is about the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial before you today.’”

verse.text: But Felix, who was rather well informed about the Way, adjourned the hearing, saying, “When Lysias the commander comes down, I will decide your case.”
verse.note: The word is literally 'leader of a thousand' and was the standard Greek term for a Roman military tribune. Here it means the officer in command of the cohort stationed in Jerusalem. 'Tribune' is the more technical rendering used by several translations.

verse.text: He ordered the centurion to keep Paul under guard but to allow him some freedom, and not to prevent any of his own people from attending to his needs.
Some days later Felix came with his wife Drusilla, who was Jewish, and he sent for Paul and listened to him speak about faith in Christ Jesus.

note.term: his wife Drusilla, who was Jewish

verse.note: Drusilla was the youngest daughter of Herod Agrippa I, whose death is told in Acts 12. According to Josephus, Felix persuaded her to leave her first husband, the king of Emesa, to marry him. Readers who knew this would hear a pointed edge in Paul's topics in verse 25.

verse.text: But as Paul discussed righteousness, self-control, and the coming judgment, Felix became afraid and replied, “That is enough for now; go. When I find an opportunity I will send for you.”
verse.note: Greek has one word-family where English has two: righteous and just, righteousness and justice. Here, addressed to a governor who sat as judge and who hoped for a bribe (verse 26), the word could equally be heard as 'justice'. The same family lies behind 'the righteous and the unrighteous' in verse 15, which older versions render 'the just and unjust'.

verse.text: At the same time he was also hoping that Paul would give him money, and so he sent for him quite often and talked with him.
When two years had passed, Felix was succeeded by Porcius Festus; and because he wanted to gain favor with the Jews, Felix left Paul in prison.
Three days after Festus arrived in the province, he went up to Jerusalem from Caesarea,
and the chief priests and the leading men of the Jews presented their case against Paul to him. They kept urging him,
asking as a favor against Paul that he summon him to Jerusalem; they were setting an ambush to kill him on the way.
Festus answered that Paul was being kept at Caesarea, and that he himself was about to leave for there shortly.
“So let those among you who have authority,” he said, “come down with me, and if there is anything wrong in the man, let them accuse him.”
After spending no more than eight or ten days among them, he went down to Caesarea, and the next day he sat on the judgment seat and ordered Paul to be brought.
verse.note: The word names the raised platform on which a Roman magistrate sat to hear cases. Taking his seat there marked the proceedings as a formal trial, which is why Paul can say in verse 10 that he already stands before Caesar's court: the governor judged as the emperor's representative.

verse.text: When he arrived, the Jews who had come down from Jerusalem stood around him, bringing many serious charges that they were not able to prove,
while Paul said in his defense, “I have committed no offense against the law of the Jews, or against the temple, or against Caesar.”
But Festus, wishing to do the Jews a favor, answered Paul, “Are you willing to go up to Jerusalem and be tried there about these matters before me?”
Paul said, “I am standing before Caesar’s judgment seat, where I ought to be tried. I have done the Jews no wrong, as you yourself know very well.

text.q: If, then, I am in the wrong and have done anything deserving death, I do not refuse to die. But if there is nothing in what these men accuse me of, no one can hand me over to them as a favor. I appeal to Caesar.”

note.term: hand me over to them as a favor

verse.note: The verb means to grant something as a favor, and it shares its root with the noun for the 'favor' the leaders asked for in verse 3 and that Festus wished to do in verse 9. Most versions say only 'hand me over' or 'deliver me', which loses Paul's pointed echo. Festus uses the same verb in verse 16.

A Roman citizen facing a capital charge could have his case transferred from a provincial governor to the emperor's court in Rome. The emperor at this time was Nero. The exact legal scope of the right in this period is debated, which may be why Festus consults his advisers before granting it.

verse.text: Then Festus, after conferring with his council, answered, “You have appealed to Caesar; to Caesar you will go.”
After some days had passed, King Agrippa and Bernice arrived at Caesarea to pay their respects to Festus.
verse.note: This is Herod Agrippa II, son of the Herod of Acts 12 and great-grandson of Herod the Great. He ruled territories to the north-east under Roman patronage and had authority over the Jerusalem temple and the appointment of high priests. Bernice was his sister. A courtesy visit to a newly arrived governor was expected of a client king.

verse.text: As they were spending several days there, Festus laid Paul’s case before the king, saying, “There is a man left behind by Felix as a prisoner.

text.q: When I was in Jerusalem, the chief priests and the elders of the Jews presented their case about him, asking for a sentence against him.

I answered them that it is not the custom of Romans to hand over any person as a favor before the accused has met his accusers face to face and had an opportunity to defend himself against the accusation.
So when they had come together here, I made no delay: the next day I sat on the judgment seat and ordered the man to be brought.
When the accusers stood up, they brought against him no charge of the crimes I had suspected.

note.term: of the crimes I had suspected
note.traditional: of such things as I supposed

verse.note: Manuscripts differ over the word for 'evil' here: some make it describe the things suspected, some make it describe the charge, and some omit it. The reading translated has 'evil things', meaning serious crimes. The sense of the verse is much the same on any reading.

text.q: Instead they had certain disputes with him about their own religion and about a certain Jesus, who had died, but whom Paul claimed to be alive.

verse.note: The Greek word could be used neutrally or respectfully for devotion to the gods, or dismissively for superstition. Older versions have 'superstition'. Most modern translators choose 'religion' because Festus is speaking to a Jewish king whom he would not wish to insult. A Roman official's private view may still have been closer to the dismissive sense.

text.q: Being at a loss how to investigate these matters, I asked whether he would be willing to go to Jerusalem and be tried there about them.
But when Paul appealed to be kept for the Emperor’s decision, I ordered him to be kept until I could send him up to Caesar.”

verse.note: The Greek title is the standard equivalent of the Latin Augustus, 'the revered one'. It was first given to Octavian and then borne by each emperor after him. Here it refers to the reigning emperor, Nero, not to the first Augustus, so 'the Emperor' is used, while 'Caesar' is kept for the other word.

verse.text: Agrippa said to Festus, “I would like to hear the man myself.” “Tomorrow,” he said, “you will hear him.”

So the next day Agrippa and Bernice came with great pageantry and entered the audience hall with the military tribunes and the most prominent men of the city, and at Festus’s command Paul was brought in.
verse.note: The Greek term, literally 'commander of a thousand', was the regular equivalent of the Roman military tribune, the officer commanding a cohort. Those present would be the senior officers of the units stationed at Caesarea, the governor's headquarters.

verse.text: And Festus said, “King Agrippa, and all you men who are present with us, you see this man about whom the whole multitude of the Jews petitioned me, both in Jerusalem and here, shouting that he must not live any longer.

text.q: But I found that he had done nothing deserving death, and when he himself appealed to the Emperor, I decided to send him.

I have nothing definite to write to my lord about him. So I have brought him before all of you, and especially before you, King Agrippa, so that after the examination has taken place I may have something to write.

verse.note: The Greek has simply 'the lord', used as a title for the emperor. The usage became common in the eastern provinces around this time. It is the same word that Christians used for Jesus, and readers of Acts would have noticed that.

text.q: For it seems unreasonable to me to send a prisoner without also indicating the charges against him.”

verse.text: Agrippa said to Paul, “You are permitted to speak for yourself.” Then Paul stretched out his hand and began his defense:

text.q: “Concerning everything I am accused of by Jews, King Agrippa, I consider myself blessed that it is before you I am to make my defense today,

verse.note: Most translations render the word here as 'fortunate' or 'happy', treating it as a courtesy in a speech's opening. It is the same word as in the Beatitudes, and this translation renders it 'blessed' throughout so the reader can see that. In this context the sense is close to 'fortunate'.

text.q: especially since you are an expert in all the customs and controversies of the Jews. So I beg you to hear me patiently.
My manner of life from my youth, spent from the beginning among my own nation and in Jerusalem, is known to all Jews.

verse.note: The Greek word here is the same one translated 'Gentiles' in verses 17, 20 and 23. In the singular it means a people or nation, here Paul's own Jewish people. In the plural it usually means the non-Jewish peoples.

text.q: They have known me from far back, if they are willing to testify, that I lived as a Pharisee, according to the strictest party of our religion.

verse.note: The word means a school or party within a larger body, and was used neutrally of philosophical schools and of Jewish groups such as the Pharisees and Sadducees. 'Sect' now suggests a breakaway or fringe group, which is not implied here. Many translations still use 'sect'.

text.q: And now I stand here being judged for hope in the promise God made to our fathers,
the promise our twelve tribes hope to attain as they earnestly worship night and day. It is about this hope, O king, that I am accused by Jews!
Why is it judged unbelievable among you that God raises the dead?
I myself was convinced that I ought to do many things against the name of Jesus of Nazareth.
And that is what I did in Jerusalem. I locked up many of the holy ones in prisons, having received authority from the chief priests, and when they were being put to death I cast my vote against them.

verse.note: The traditional rendering is 'saints', which now suggests canonised individuals or people of unusual virtue. The word is used of all believers as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint's language for Israel. Many translations keep 'saints'; others use 'God's people'.

note.traditional: gave my voice against them / cast my vote against them

verse.note: Literally 'I brought down a pebble', from the practice of voting with pebbles. Whether this means Paul was a voting member of the Sanhedrin or is a figure of speech for his approval, as at Stephen's death, is disputed.

text.q: In all the synagogues I often punished them and tried to force them to blaspheme, and, raging madly against them beyond all measure, I persecuted them even as far as foreign cities.

note.term: tried to force them to blaspheme

verse.note: The Greek tense can describe a repeated action ('I kept forcing them') or an attempted one ('I tried to force them'). Most modern translations take it as an attempt, without implying that it succeeded. The blasphemy meant is presumably cursing or renouncing Jesus.

text.q: In the course of this I was traveling to Damascus with the authority and commission of the chief priests,
when at midday on the road, O king, I saw a light from heaven, brighter than the sun, shining around me and those traveling with me.
We all fell to the ground, and I heard a voice saying to me in the Hebrew language,
‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It is hard for you to kick against the goads.’

verse.note: The Greek expression can refer to Hebrew or to Aramaic, the everyday language of many Jews in Judea and Galilee. Many scholars think Aramaic is meant, and some translations say so, but this is not certain. The form of the name, 'Saoul', reflects the Semitic original.

A goad is a pointed stick for driving oxen; an animal that kicks back at it only hurts itself. The phrase was a well-known Greek proverb for futile resistance to a greater power, especially a divine one, and is found in writers such as Euripides. It is about the futility of resisting. The words themselves do not point to a troubled conscience.

text.q: I said, ‘Who are you, Lord?’ And the Lord said,
‘I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.
But get up and stand on your feet. For this is why I have appeared to you: to appoint you a servant and a witness both of what you have seen of me and of the things in which I will appear to you,
rescuing you from the people and from the Gentiles, to whom I am sending you
to open their eyes, so that they turn from darkness to light and from the authority of Satan to God, and so that they receive forgiveness of sins and a share among those made holy by faith in me.’
So then, King Agrippa, I was not disobedient to the heavenly vision,

but first to those in Damascus and in Jerusalem, and throughout the whole region of Judea, and to the Gentiles, I declared that they should turn back and turn to God, doing deeds worthy of that turning back.

verse.note: The traditional rendering is 'repent', with 'repentance' for the related noun at the end of the verse. 'Repent' now centres on feeling sorry, whereas the word carries the prophets' call to return to God in mind and conduct. It is paired here with a second verb meaning simply 'turn'. Most translations keep 'repent' as an established term.

text.q: For this reason Jews seized me in the temple and tried to kill me.
So, having received help from God, I stand to this day testifying to both small and great, saying nothing beyond what the prophets and Moses said was going to happen:
that the Messiah was to suffer, and that, as the first to rise from the dead, he was to proclaim light both to the people and to the Gentiles.”

verse.note: The Greek word is the one usually rendered 'Christ'. Here it is a title, the anointed king Israel expected, and the point in dispute is whether that figure was to suffer, so 'Messiah' is used. Several modern translations make the same distinction in the Gospels and Acts.

verse.text: As he was saying these things in his defense, Festus said in a loud voice, “You are mad, Paul! Your great learning is driving you to madness.”
But Paul said, “I am not mad, most excellent Festus. I am uttering words of truth and sound sense.

text.q: For the king knows about these things, and to him I speak freely; for I am not persuaded that any of this escapes him, since this was not done in a corner.
Do you believe the prophets, King Agrippa? I know that you believe.”

verse.text: Agrippa said to Paul, “In so short a time you are persuading me to play the Christian!”

note.traditional: Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian

verse.note: Agrippa's reply is difficult in Greek. It can mean 'you are persuading me to act the Christian', by an idiom with a Septuagint parallel, or 'you are trying to persuade me, so as to make me a Christian'. The opening phrase can mean 'in a short time' or 'with little effort'; the older 'almost' is now generally rejected. His tone, whether ironic, evasive or serious, is not marked, and Paul's answer picks up the same phrase.

verse.text: Paul replied, “Whether in a short time or a long one, I would pray to God that not only you but all who are listening to me today might become such as I am, apart from these chains.”
Then the king rose, and the governor and Bernice and those seated with them,
and after they had withdrawn they were saying to one another, “This man is doing nothing that deserves death or chains.”
Agrippa said to Festus, “This man could have been released if he had not appealed to Caesar.”
When it was decided that we should sail for Italy, they handed Paul and some other prisoners over to a centurion named Julius, of the Augustan Cohort.
verse.note: The narrative returns here to the first person plural, last used when Paul arrived in Jerusalem (21:18), and keeps it through the voyage to Rome. The traditional explanation is that the author, or a source he used, was a companion of Paul on the journey. Some scholars regard the 'we' as a literary convention, but that view is a minority one.

A cohort was a unit of several hundred soldiers. 'Augustan' was an honorific title granted to some auxiliary units of the Roman army. A unit with this title appears to have been stationed in the region in the first century, though which one Julius belonged to is not certain.

verse.text: We boarded a ship from Adramyttium that was about to sail to the ports along the coast of Asia, and we put out to sea; Aristarchus, a Macedonian from Thessalonica, was with us.
The next day we put in at Sidon, and Julius treated Paul kindly and allowed him to go to his friends and be cared for.
Putting out from there, we sailed under the lee of Cyprus, because the winds were against us,
and after sailing across the open sea off Cilicia and Pamphylia, we came down to Myra in Lycia.
There the centurion found an Alexandrian ship sailing for Italy and put us aboard it.
For a good many days we sailed slowly and with difficulty arrived off Cnidus; then, since the wind would not let us go on, we sailed under the lee of Crete off Salmone,
and coasting along it with difficulty we came to a place called Fair Havens, near the city of Lasea.
Since a good deal of time had passed and the voyage was now dangerous, because even the Fast had already gone by, Paul advised them,
verse.note: The Fast is the Day of Atonement, which falls in late September or early October. Ancient sailors regarded the open Mediterranean as dangerous from mid-September and as closed to shipping over the winter. Luke's point is that the safe season had run out.

verse.text: saying to them, “Men, I can see that the voyage is going to bring disaster and heavy loss, not only of the cargo and the ship but also of our lives.”
But the centurion was persuaded by the pilot and the ship’s owner rather than by what Paul said.

Since the harbor was unsuitable for wintering in, the majority decided to put out from there, in the hope that they could somehow reach Phoenix, a harbor of Crete facing southwest and northwest, and winter there.

note.traditional: lieth toward the south west and north west

verse.note: The Greek says literally that the harbor 'looks along the southwest wind and along the northwest wind'. This may mean it faces those directions, that is, opens to the west. It may instead mean it looks the way those winds blow, that is, toward the northeast and southeast. The identification of Phoenix on the south coast of Crete is disputed, and the choice depends partly on which site is meant.

verse.text: When a gentle south wind began to blow, they thought they had achieved their purpose; they weighed anchor and coasted along Crete, close inshore.
But before long a wind of hurricane force, the one called the Northeaster, swept down from the island.
verse.note: The best manuscripts give the name Eurakylon, a sailors' compound of the Greek for the east wind and the Latin for the north wind, meaning a wind from the east-northeast. It is translated here because the name tells an English reader nothing. Later manuscripts read Euroclydon, which is the form in the King James Version.

verse.text: The ship was caught by it and could not head into the wind, so we gave way and were driven along.
Running under the lee of a small island called Cauda, we managed with difficulty to get the ship’s boat under control.
After hoisting it aboard, they used cables to undergird the ship; and fearing that they would run aground on the Syrtis, they lowered the gear and so were driven along.
verse.note: The Syrtis was a stretch of shallows and shifting sandbanks off the coast of North Africa, in the gulfs of modern Libya and Tunisia. Ancient sailors dreaded it. It lay far to the southwest, and a northeast gale would drive a ship straight toward it.

note.traditional: strake sail (KJV); lowered the sea anchor

verse.note: The Greek word is a general term for equipment, and Luke does not say which piece is meant. It may mean that the crew lowered the mainsail and its yard. It may instead mean that they let out a drag or sea anchor to slow the ship's drift. The translation leaves the term as general as the Greek.

verse.text: As we were being violently battered by the storm, the next day they began throwing cargo overboard,
and on the third day they threw the ship’s tackle overboard with their own hands.
When neither sun nor stars appeared for many days, and no small storm lay upon us, all hope of our being saved was at last being taken away.
verse.note: The verb is the one used elsewhere in the New Testament for salvation in the religious sense. Throughout this chapter (also verses 31, 34, 43 and 44) it and its related words refer to rescue from the sea. Many interpreters think Luke means the reader to hear the wider resonance, but the plain sense here is physical survival.

verse.text: When they had gone a long time without food, Paul stood up among them and said, “Men, you should have listened to me and not put out from Crete, and so been spared this disaster and loss.

text.q: And now I advise you to take heart, for there will be no loss of life among you, only of the ship.
For last night there stood beside me an angel of the God to whom I belong and whom I also serve,
saying,
‘Do not be afraid, Paul. You must stand before Caesar; and look, God has graciously given you all who are sailing with you.’
So take heart, men, for I believe God that it will be exactly as I have been told.
But we must run aground on some island.”

verse.text: When the fourteenth night came, as we were being driven across the Sea of Adria, about midnight the sailors began to suspect that they were nearing land.
verse.note: In the first century 'Adria' covered far more than the modern Adriatic. It included the central Mediterranean between Crete and Greece on one side and Sicily and Malta on the other. 'Adriatic' would wrongly place the ship between Italy and the Balkans, so the older form of the name is kept.

verse.text: They took a sounding and found twenty fathoms; a little farther on they took another sounding and found fifteen fathoms.
Fearing that we might run aground somewhere on the rocks, they dropped four anchors from the stern and prayed for day to come.
But when the sailors tried to escape from the ship and lowered the ship’s boat into the sea, on the pretext that they were going to lay out anchors from the bow,
Paul said to the centurion and the soldiers, “Unless these men stay on the ship, you cannot be saved.”
Then the soldiers cut the ropes of the ship’s boat and let it fall away.
Until day was about to break, Paul kept urging them all to take some food, saying, “Today is the fourteenth day that you have been waiting in suspense and going without food, taking nothing.

text.q: So I urge you to take some food, for this is for your survival; not a hair will perish from the head of any of you.”

verse.text: Having said this, he took bread, gave thanks to God in front of them all, broke it, and began to eat.

note.term: took bread, gave thanks to God

verse.note: Taking bread, giving thanks and breaking it is how any Jewish meal began. It is also the sequence Luke uses for the feeding of the five thousand and the Last Supper. Scholars are divided on whether he intends an allusion to the Lord's Supper here. Most see an ordinary meal described in deliberately familiar language, since the company was largely non-Christian.

verse.text: Then they all took heart and took food themselves.
In all we were two hundred seventy-six persons on the ship.
verse.note: A few early witnesses read 'about seventy-six' instead. The difference is very small in Greek and probably arose from a copying slip. The larger number is well within the capacity of an Alexandrian grain ship and is accepted by nearly all editors.

verse.text: When they had eaten their fill, they began to lighten the ship by throwing the grain out into the sea.
When day came, they did not recognize the land, but they noticed a bay with a beach, and they planned to run the ship ashore on it if they could.
So they cast off the anchors and left them in the sea, at the same time loosening the ropes that held the steering oars; then, hoisting the foresail to the wind, they made for the beach.
But they struck a place where two seas met and ran the vessel aground; the bow stuck fast and remained immovable, while the stern was being broken up by the pounding.

note.term: a place where two seas met
note.traditional: a place where two seas met

verse.note: The Greek adjective means roughly 'with sea on both sides' or 'between two seas'. It could describe a sandbar or shoal with deep water on either side, a spit of land, or a channel where currents meet. Many modern versions render it 'sandbar' or 'reef'. The translation keeps the more literal phrase because the exact feature is uncertain.

verse.text: The soldiers’ plan was to kill the prisoners, so that none of them would swim away and escape;
but the centurion, wanting to bring Paul safely through, kept them from carrying out the plan. He ordered those who could swim to jump overboard first and make for land,
and the rest to follow, some on planks and some on pieces of the ship. And so it came about that all were brought safely to land.
verse.note: The Greek says literally 'on some of the things from the ship', or equally 'on some of those from the ship'. The second reading would mean that non-swimmers were carried ashore by members of the crew. Most translators take it of wreckage, as here, but the grammar allows either.

verse.text: When we had been brought safely through, we then learned that the island was called Malta.
The natives showed us no ordinary kindness: they lit a fire and welcomed us all, because of the rain that had set in and because of the cold.
verse.note: The Greek word described anyone who did not speak Greek and carried no necessary suggestion of savagery; the Maltese of this period largely spoke a Punic dialect. "Barbarians" now implies brutality, which the verse itself contradicts by praising their kindness. Most modern translations likewise use "natives" or "islanders".

verse.text: When Paul had gathered a bundle of brushwood and put it on the fire, a viper came out because of the heat and fastened onto his hand.

When the natives saw the creature hanging from his hand, they said to one another, “This man must certainly be a murderer. Though he was brought safely out of the sea, Justice has not allowed him to live.”
verse.note: The islanders speak of justice as a personal power that pursues the guilty. Greek tradition personified it as the goddess Dike, and the speakers may have in mind her or a local equivalent. Older versions render it "vengeance"; most modern ones capitalize "Justice".

verse.text: He, however, shook the creature off into the fire and suffered no harm.

They were expecting him to swell up or suddenly fall down dead. But after they had waited a long time and saw nothing out of the ordinary happening to him, they changed their minds and began to say he was a god.
In the area around that place there were estates belonging to the leading man of the island, named Publius, who welcomed us and entertained us hospitably for three days.

note.term: the leading man of the island
note.traditional: the chief man of the island

verse.note: Literally "the first man of the island." This appears to be a recognized local title, not just a description, and inscriptions from Malta are usually cited as attesting it. Whether Publius was the senior Roman official or the foremost local benefactor is not certain.

verse.text: It happened that Publius’s father was lying ill, suffering from bouts of fever and dysentery. Paul went in to him, prayed, laid his hands on him, and healed him.
After this happened, the rest of the people on the island who had illnesses also kept coming and were cured.
They also honored us with many honors, and when we were putting out to sea they put on board what we needed.
After three months we put out to sea in a ship that had wintered at the island, an Alexandrian ship with the Dioscuri as its emblem.

note.traditional: Castor and Pollux / the Twin Brothers

verse.note: The Dioscuri ("sons of Zeus") were the twin gods Castor and Pollux, widely regarded as protectors of sailors. Ships carried a carved or painted emblem at the bow that served as their name, so this ship was in effect called "The Dioscuri."

verse.text: We put in at Syracuse and stayed three days.
From there we weighed anchor and reached Rhegium. After one day a south wind came up, and on the second day we came to Puteoli,

note.traditional: fetched a compass / made a circuit / set sail

verse.note: The manuscripts are divided between a word meaning "taking away" (understood as casting off or raising the anchors, as in 27:40) and a very similar word meaning "going around," which would describe a tacking or circuitous course. The edition translated here adopts the first. The sense of either reading in this nautical context is somewhat uncertain.

verse.text: where we found brothers and were invited to stay with them for seven days. And so we came to Rome.
The brothers from there, having heard about us, came as far as the Forum of Appius and Three Taverns to meet us. When Paul saw them, he gave thanks to God and took courage.

note.term: the Forum of Appius and Three Taverns
note.traditional: Appii Forum and The Three Taverns

verse.note: These were two stopping places on the Appian Way, the main road south from Rome, roughly forty and thirty miles from the city. Believers from Rome travelled a day or more on foot to escort Paul in, a courtesy normally shown to an arriving dignitary.

verse.text: When we entered Rome, Paul was permitted to stay by himself, with the soldier who guarded him.

Three days later he called together the leading men of the Jews. When they had gathered, he said to them, “Brothers, I have done nothing against the people or our ancestral customs, yet I was handed over from Jerusalem as a prisoner into the hands of the Romans,

text.q: who, after examining me, wanted to release me, because there was no ground for a death sentence in my case.
But when the Jews spoke against this, I was forced to appeal to Caesar, though not because I had any charge to bring against my nation.

verse.note: The Greek word here is the same one translated "Gentiles" in verse 28. In the singular it means a people or nation, here Israel; in the plural it commonly means the non-Jewish peoples. English has no single word that covers both uses.

text.q: For this reason, then, I asked to see you and speak with you, for it is because of the hope of Israel that I wear this chain.”

verse.text: They said to him, “We have received no letters about you from Judea, nor has any of the brothers who came here reported or said anything bad about you.

text.q: But we would like to hear from you what your views are, for as regards this sect, we know that it is spoken against everywhere.”

verse.text: They set a day with him and came to him at his lodging in greater numbers. From morning until evening he laid the matter out for them, bearing solemn witness to the kingdom of God and trying to persuade them about Jesus from both the Law of Moses and the Prophets.
Some were persuaded by what was said, but others refused to believe.
Disagreeing among themselves, they began to leave after Paul had said one thing: “The Holy Spirit spoke rightly through Isaiah the prophet to your ancestors,

text.q: saying, ‘Go to this people and say: You will hear and hear but never understand, and you will look and look but never see.

note.traditional: Hearing you will hear / You will indeed hear

verse.note: Paul quotes Isaiah 6:9–10 in the wording of the Greek Septuagint. The doubled expressions ("with hearing you will hear," "looking you will look") reproduce a Hebrew idiom of emphasis. The same passage is quoted in the Gospels to explain why many did not respond to Jesus.

text.q: For the heart of this people has grown dull, and with their ears they have become hard of hearing, and their eyes they have shut; otherwise they might see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart and turn back, and I would heal them.’
So let it be known to you that this salvation of God has been sent to the Gentiles, and they will indeed hear.”

verse.text: He stayed two whole years at his own expense and welcomed all who came to him,
verse.note: Verse 29 is absent from the earliest manuscripts and is not printed in the Greek edition translated here. Later manuscripts add: "And when he had said these things, the Jews departed, having a great dispute among themselves." Most scholars regard it as a later addition to smooth the transition.

Elsewhere the Greek noun means a price or rent paid, which gives "at his own expense." Many translations render it "in his own rented house," which fits the verb "stayed" naturally but is a sense not clearly attested for this word outside this verse. Either way, Paul was paying for private lodging while under guard.

verse.text: proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with complete boldness, unhindered.
